subsubtopic: INDIA-PAKISTAN  ANNOUNCEMENT OF SETTLE- MENT RESPECTING INDUS WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that on July 9 of last year I announced with respect to the Indus waters 79951-0-97
question that the Canadian government had agreed in principle to participate in the program that had been drawn up by the international bank on the understanding that the funds required for this purpose would be provided as part of our increased Colombo plan contribution. I said on that occasion that I was confident that the house would endorse the government's view that it was in Canada's interest to help in the solution of a problem which has stood in the way of better relations between two of our commonwealth partners in Asia.
It is a matter of great satisfaction to me to be able to inform the house that good progress has been made in working toward a solution of the Indus waters question acceptable to the two states concerned, India and Pakistan. These discussions have now reached the point where the bank and those countries, including Canada, which joined together to help in reaching a mutually acceptable solution have agreed that an announcement on the Indus settlement should be made today by the international bank in Washington. The bank's announcement will give full details of the proposed settlement. Meanwhile I should like to mention the major points briefly.
The Canadian government, subject to the ratification of a water treaty between India and Pakistan now under negotiation, has agreed to contribute $22.1 million (Canadian) over the next ten years to the program for the development of the Indus waters. Parliament will be requested to approve this grant at the appropriate time.
In addition to the large loan which the bank has agreed to make, Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States and Germany have all agreed to contribute funds; the United States has offered to provide additional sums through loans, and India and Pakistan will each make substantial contributions.
The proposed development program provides for the construction of very large works which will divide the waters of the Indus in accordance with the treaty which India and Pakistan are currently negotiating. It is estimated that it will take 10 years to complete this project, which will provide water for irrigation and land reclamation, and important potential hydroelectric power resources as well as flood control works.

External Affairs
I am sure I speak for all members of the house when I say how gratified I am at the progress which India and Pakistan, with the resourceful help of the bank, have made in working toward a settlement of this question. With the continued good will which has characterized the discussions so far, I am hopeful and confident that full agreement will be reached and that a new and important phase in the development of the great potential resources of these countries will be opened.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN SCOPE OF ACT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing a comprehensive system of national health insurance, more particularly to give consideration to the advisability of: (a) amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to provide benefits on behalf of patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and patients confined to mental institutions; (b) introducing legislation to provide medical, dental and optical insurance.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to introduce this resolution I have in mind the problems that have faced the Canadian people in the past in regard to health insurance, and the work that has been done by governments in the past in investigating the possibilities of establishing a plan in Canada and some of the results that have been achieved.
Throughout the lifetime of the C.C.F. it has been our hope that we would be able to have implemented in Canada an insurance plan that would cover all the costs of health care for all the people in Canada, regardless of the amount of that cost. On many occasions we have been faced with the problem of Canadian people receiving medical and hospital care in relation to their wealth. As the costs of health care increase it becomes increasingly necessary that some form of health insurance be implemented in Canada to take care of the needs of those people who are less able to finance a plan of their own.
Over a period of years health insurance programs have become somewhat common in Canada. The federal government now has a hospitalization plan which has been put into effect without interfering with the British North America Act or with provincial jurisdiction in this particular field. We have gone into hospital insurance to the extent that most of the provinces in Canada have joined in the plan, and even those that are not now in are contemplating implementing some type of hospital insurance for themselves.
We believe that the federal government, which has given the lead to some of the provinces in this particular field, should also give a lead in completing the coverage of free health insurance to all the people of Canada. The responsibilities of the provincial and federal governments have been completely established in this field, and I quote from the reference book for the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, 1945. Under the heading "Division of Responsibilities" we find the following:
Jurisdiction respecting public health is based upon the British North America Act. 1867, and all health activities are conducted within the limitations of the statutory jurisdiction laid down by that act. To the dominion government was assigned jurisdiction over "quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals'', and to the provinces "the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions in and for the provinces, other than marine hospitals". But the residuary power for public health has been generally accepted as being in the province by virtue of provincial jurisdiction over "property and civil rights in the province" and "generally all matters of a merely local or private nature in the province".
In this study that was inaugurated by a previous Liberal government some time was taken in consideration of some of the problems that have arisen through the implementation of hospital plans and other types of plans throughout the country, plans that were being discussed at that time. It was generally conceded that it was not necessary to have unanimity amongst the provinces as to the coverage that would be afforded, and that coverage could be granted by the federal government as was done in the case of hospital insurance.
Before we go into some of the other aspects of health insurance I think it would be interesting to note some of the things that have happened in the hospitalization field. A plan of hospital insurance was implemented in Saskatchewan in 1946, under which the provincial government took full responsibility for the plan. In their election promises that year they indicated that if any assistance was made available from the federal government it was their intention to put into effect a complete health insurance plan in that province. The federal government made certain proposals in the dominion-provincial conferences of that day. They instituted studies of the matter, and indicated to the voters in 1945 particularly that they would consider some kind of complete health insurance. Saskatchewan carried their plan for a number of years, and later the federal government did come into the plan in various ways as requested by the province.

It seems to me that some of the provinces that have put hospital insurance into effect have not wanted hospital insurance at all, but have met a demand by the people themselves for this type of coverage. The plan in Ontario is probably a good example, because we find that many people who were brought under the hospitalization plan in that province on a voluntary basis are now suffering a great deal of hardship because of the inefficiency of the method of collecting money for the particular plan. I have received quite a number of letters from people who thought their medical plan was prepaid, inasmuch at it was prepaid originally for three months. They thought their former Blue Cross plan was being carried into effect. The fact of the matter is that in most cases these people received no notification that their next payment was due. After the three month period had expired they received letters saying that they were no longer under the plan, and that they could reapply if they wished but there would be another three month waiting period.
Therefore it would appear, as has been suggested many times, that if the people putting a hospital insurance or complete health insurance program into effect do not believe the plan is one that should be and can be applied to all the people, there will be ineffectual coverage; the plan will not be the success that it could be if it were implemented by people who believe that the idea of health insurance is to give coverage to all people regardless of their ability to pay or their wage structure, and that everybody should have the advantages of the plan.
These are the types of problems that have developed. I think the problem in Ontario can be solved; but it is an indication that if these plans are not put into effect by people who believe in them, many problems can develop that should not develop, and this is certainly true in the province of Ontario at the present time. I should like to quote one article from Comment which contains the following:
One of the most revealing, although not surprising, features of the Canadian sickness survey, the results of which were published last year, is that low income groups get less medical care although they have proportionately more illnesses. The report states:
"While the low income group reported proportionately far more disabling illness than other income groups, they received much less physicians' care. In relation to the number of days of disability reported, persons in the low income groups received on the average only about half of the amount of physicians' care received by persons in the medium income group and only two fifths of the amount received by persons in the high income group. The low income group reported 8.78 doctors' calls and clinic visits per 100 disability days, as against 16.82 for the medium income group and 20.78 for the high income group.
Health Insurance
"In relation to disability days reported the low income group received the least of graduate nursing care-0.39 visits per 100 disability days. The medium income group received a little more (0.42 visits per 100 disability days), but a considerably greater amount was received by the high income group (0.61 visits per 100 disability days)".
It was the same story with dental care.
"Only 9.1 per cent of persons in the low income group visited a dentist during the year, as against 14.0 per cent of the medium income group and 19.3 per cent of the high income group".
Likewise for miscellaneous health care.
"The low income group reported 78 miscellaneous treatments per 1,000 persons which was about half the number reported by the medium and high income groups (150 and 155 per 1,000 persons respectively)".
We can all remember back to the days of the last war, when a large number of people were entering the services. Many of them were considered to be suffering from malnutrition, and others from medical problems that could and should have been corrected when they were in their growing years. In Canada the proportion of those who had to be turned down for military service because of their inability to obtain proper medical, dental and optical care during the years when it was needed most was much greater than in many other countries. Canada being the large and progressive country that it is, it seems to me that we in Canada can afford the best type of health care for all our people irrespective of their earning power; and that if we can afford this care we should be able to supply it. It was for this reason that I introduced this particular resolution.
The history of the rich and the poor in relationship to health care was pointed out in the proposals of the government of Canada in August of 1945 to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction. At page 28 of the green book they pointed out:
There are great inequalities in the quantity and quality of health care available to different groups of Canadians, and in the costs of such public and private health services and medical and hospital facilities as are now available. These inequalities in part reflect differences in personal incomes, and in part are due to differences between rural and urban areas. Great differences between provinces arise from these same factors.
Then it goes on to say this:
Under our present system, for the man who car afford to pay, the cost of ill-health falls at the very moment when his earning capacity is cut off. The cost of treatment and cure for the individual who cannot afford to pay is borne to a considerable degree through the benefactions of well to do members of the community and the generosity of doctors who give so freely of their time and skill, and more and more by the provincial governments and municipalities. In spite of these efforts desirable treatment is still not obtained in many cases. While much of the cost of illness is thus hidden, it can only come out of the total productive capacity of the country. The advantages of a broader provision of health services on a more equitable basis are obvious.

Health Insurance
It goes on to say this:
There are also wide variations in the quality of services across Canada-widely varying patient-day costs, patient-doctor ratios and salary ranges in hospitals. There are just as great variations in the incidence of tuberculosis, venereal disease and other communicable diseases.
To remove the disparities in standards of health services in different parts of Canada, to avoid the risks of sudden heavy expenditures, and distribute health costs more widely and equitably, and above all, to obtain the benefits of better health for the great majority of our people- these are the objects of the proposals which the federal government is now making with respect to health insurance for all, and increased public health services assisted by federal grants.
We are fortunate today-and I say that with my tongue in my cheek, probably-that we still have in the house with us the former minister of national health and welfare. I am quite sure that in speaking on this resolution he will point out that if his government had remained in office these things would have come to pass. However, let me point out that he was also the minister of national health and welfare from the time these proposals were made in 1945 until 1957, and that very little was done. I am also pleased to say that his consideration at this time hinged on the fact that the provinces were all going to have to co-operate before anything was done. I am happy to say that he had a change of heart in later days, and that these services were provided in the hospital field when the majority of the provinces indicated their desire for those services.
However, I would suggest that his party promised health insurance since 1919 and we are still asking for it, as is obvious by this resolution. If it had been provided, this resolution would have asked for an increase in some of the services that were provided under a health insurance scheme, and we would not have had to ask for basic coverage.
Over the years Conservative governments also have made many attempts to provide the electors with a health insurance program before elections; but, singularly, they have made very few proposals after they were elected. I should like to use the example of Ontario. In Ontario there was a Conservative government at that time; and not only were there the Progressive Conservatives in Ontario but there were the Union Nationale and Social Credit governments in other provinces than Ontario; and the only province which expressed any desire for health insurance on a broad scale was the province of Saskatchewan. The Ontario Conservatives promised to launch a provincial health program in 1943 when Mr. Drew, in announcing his 22-point program to the electors of the day, promised as his second point in that program-and he indicated that it was extremely important by putting it at the top-as follows:

2. We will at all times work In effective co-operation with the dominion government and with all other governing bodies in Canada in all activities which will assist in the prosecution of the war to a successful conclusion, and in establishing a sound basis of social security, health insurance and protection in their old age for all our people.
Section 11, dealing directly with health insurance, said this:
Health measures will be established so that medical, dental and other health protection will be available for all.
That was reported in the Toronto Daily Star of July 9, 1943. Yet Mr. Drew came and went. The 22 proposals in Ontario were dusted off and added to many times, and this proposal is just as good in the province of Ontario today as it was then because it has been implemented only to a very limited extent. With the Conservative government now at Ottawa, and having among its members some who sat in the Ontario house at that time, I hope they are going to indicate that at that time they believed in those 22 proposals and that some of them will be rising in their places and saying they are still in favour of a complete health program which will accomplish what Mr. Drew in his 22 proposals indicated when he suggested that a program of medical, dental and other health care would be available for all.
This program of health insurance has been considered to be a socialist proposal that cannot be implemented. It has been considered that the socialists are dreaming when they suggest that all people in Canada, even those who are not able to pay the expenses that are incurred in hospital and medical care, should be protected, and that all people should be protected without any relationship to the amount of money they earn.
I think the Canadian people have indicated on numerous occasions that governments should have this in their election programs, that something should be done; and that they are willing to pay their share to see a health insurance program put into effect. It seems surprising to me that Saskatchewan, where there is a socialist government, should be the only province which went ahead before the federal government gave any notion or sign of participation to any degree in this plan. I believe they will suggest this year in their election program that they will give the people of Saskatchewan prepaid medical coverage to implement the hospitalization program. I think the people of Saskatchewan are aware that if they re-elect the government the plan will be implemented as they suggest it will, and I believe we should be entitled to expect over the years the same type of program which has been adopted in election compaigns in federal and provincial fields.

Great Britain entered into a social health scheme upon which many have passed comments. Some people say that you should not give eye glasses away, and there is a row going on now in Great Britain because the eye glasses are not considered satisfactory. Apparently they were too plain for some people while others were getting dark rimmed glasses, and there is talk that they should jazz them up a little more, similar to other countries where you have these paste diamond frames, and so on. But this is a country which is supplying people with eye glasses.
There are many people in Canada, certainly many students in rural schools, who need some kind of glasses, no matter what they are. They would be happy to have them no matter whether they had steel rims and were very plain looking. They need them not only to look pretty but because they have a functional use as well, but they are not supplied at the present time. This type of plan was put into force in Great Britain, and in my opinion and the opinion of the world in general this plan has been a success.
I have here a quotation from the London correspondent of the Wall Street Journal, which I suggest is not a pro-Labour publication. In the issue of November 27, 1951 it had this to say:
... one pillar of socialism-socialized medicine-is certain to remain intact... The "free" health service set up by the Labour government is so popular that it can no longer be made a political issue here.
Listen to Bert Greenaway, a postman whose route is in Chelsea ... "It's the finest thing that ever happened to this country. Since the service started my wife has had two babies and a new set of teeth after pyorrhea, the little girl got cured of mastoid with streptomycin, the boy had a broken arm x-rayed fourteen times and reset and we all had our tonsils out-without me paying a penny!"
In Clapham Junction where Greenaway lives-a thickly populated railway centre-infant mortality has dropped since the health service from 50 per 1,000 to 20 per 1,000. The working class children in the area get fresh milk, orange juice and cod liver oil for five years after birth at a minute charge, and mobile x-ray units pay regular visits.
About 95 per cent of the British people have registered with the health service. Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part in this debate on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Timiska-ming (Mr. Peters) and dealing with health insurance. Health is one of our most valuable possessions, if not indeed the most valuable of them all. Therefore, it is quite in order for the Canadian people's representatives in the House of Commons to attempt to improve the hospital insurance plan which was implemented by the former
fMr. Fairfield.]
administration, under the able and experienced direction of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).
We sometimes read in the papers or hear comments to the effect that the resolutions introduced in this house by opposition members serve no useful purpose. I do not share this view at all because I think that the discussion of a matter of vital importance can help us to prepare public opinion and convince members of the government to put into effect some of the very sensible suggestions made by members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition.
Mr. Speaker, I think moreover that the resolution of the hon. member of Timis-kaming might be considered from another point of view, in that it may serve to remind hon. members opposite of the solemn promises they made to the Canadian people in respect to hospital insurance.
The hon. member for Timiskaming possibly wanted to be funny when he said that the Liberals had been talking about hospital insurance for a long time. As I see it, he does not have to offer many excuses to as far as his own party is concerned. While the Liberals had promised this hospital insurance plan for a long time, members of the C.C.F. in this house have promised it ever since their party was founded, and, as far as I know, the C.C.F. party never had occasion at any time in our history, to keep, in the Canadian parliament, even one of the many promises they have made to the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, one thing is sure and it is this: before acting on promises and putting suggestions into effect, the former administration always gave practical thought to what the Canadian taxpayer would have to pay in taxes of all kinds if those promises were kept. In fact, it was as a result of those careful studies that the Liberal party succeeded in establishing a true social security charter for Canadians throughout this country.
I need not mention who it was that spent almost eleven years of his life, at the head of the Department of National Health and Welfare, in studying those suggestions, in drafting the legislation and in having it adopted by the house. The hon. member for Essex East has shown a measure of devotion, understanding and intelligence unexcelled by any other member of the house.
Therefore on behalf not only of the members of my group, but of the citizens of my riding and of my part of the country, I want to tell him once again all our appreciation for his very remarkable contribution in the field of social security.

I also listened with much attention to the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) who with restraint and intelligence, made some very sensible remarks.
However, he expressed fear that a comprehensive hospital insurance scheme might lead to state medecine; I do not share his point of view.
It was certainly neither in the legislator's nor in the government's mind when the act was passed, to establish state medecine in this country. It was only a matter of giving Canadians another social security legislation which would in no way hamper individual freedom.
As far as I am concerned, I admit that if ever health insurance or hospital insurance were to lead to state medicine, I would not hesitate to register disagreement.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa gave a long list of professional associations, medical associations and social welfare societies which have done, and are still doing, an extraordinary amount of work for the welfare of Canadians. Indeed, I believe that he rendered at the same time, though in rather veiled terms, a fine tribute to the former administration, because most of those organizations were furthered-in some cases even financially I think-by the Liberal government.
The hospital insurance scheme that is in force in most provinces of this country is, as everybody knows, a creation of the former administration. I therefore deplore the fact that legislation which is so beneficial for all those who lack the necessary means to be treated in our hospitals, is not yet available to people in the province of Quebec.
Oh, I know that, when the legislation was introduced in this parliament, some politicians in my province decried it as socialism. All sorts of reasons were advanced for not joining the hospital insurance scheme.
Unfortunate events have happened since the fall of 1959, as we had, among other things, the misfortune of losing one of our premiers, Mr. Duplessis, and then another, the Hon. Paul Sauve, who, to my mind, was a great Canadian. Now Mr. Sauve's attitude was completely different from that of his predecessor. By this time, there were no more cries of socialism, and it was recognized that the matter of hospital insurance for the province of Quebec would have to be considered.
This legislation has been in effect since 1957, Mr. Speaker. The hospital insurance act was passed by parliament almost three years ago,
Health Insurance
and I am very sorry that it was not until recently that thought was given to the setting up of a commission to study the hospital problem in Quebec at the same time as the possibility of having Quebec citizens benefit from the great federal hospital insurance scheme.
I hope this is not done for some unacknowledged reason, that is, the preparation of an event which is to take place in June or July, but that there is a genuine wish to have the citizens of our province benefit from a measure which is needed by most people in Quebec.
I deplore this delay for yet another reason, Mr. Speaker. It is well that the richer provinces in this country should help the poorer ones. I believe that Quebec has given its contribution in this field, and I am glad of it. But it would also be advisable that the hard-earned money of the citizens of the province should come back to them in some shape or other, because the vast majority of Quebec Canadians need this support. It is enough that none of the millions earmarked for universities are going into our province. I would like to see taxes paid by the people of Quebec return to us, as soon as possible, in the shape of hospital assistance for our province.
I bear the other provinces no grudge, who are benefiting from the help of Quebec or Ontario. I think that this is our way of contributing to national unity. Nevertheless, I think there are limits to a province letting its tax revenue go elsewhere, i.e. the money represented by the hard-earned daily wages of our workmen.
I therefore trust that it will not be long now, before the commission set up by the Quebec government-or which is about to be set up-considers the hospitalization problem in Quebec and concludes its study with a recommendation, which the next Liberal administration of the province will apply with the least possible delay.

Mr. Speaker, the question of extending the benefits of the legislation on hospital insurance to sanitaria and mental institutions, is not a new one. Hon. members of the Conservative party frequently discussed it when they were sitting on this side of the house and one of them, the much regretted Dr. Blair, former hon. member

for Lanark, always took a very intelligent view in this house in respect of the administration of such hospital insurance scheme, and that is why I am happy to pay him this tribute today.
So let me recall to my ex-colleagues who now occupy choice seats in this house, some of Dr. Blair's remarks. I should also like to recall some remarks from the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as well as certain comments made by no other than the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when we discussed the hospital insurance plan, which at the time was being proposed by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).
On March 25, 1957, Dr. Blair took part in the debate at the resolution stage, I think, and I should like to quote the following paragraph which is found on page 2647 of volume III of Hansard for 1957:
The problem of mentally ill patients-
Dr. Blair said,
-is one of our greatest problems. Owing to advanced methods of treatment it must be pointed out that the length of stay in hospital has been steadily cut down in the past 20 years, enabling the hospital to care for more patients. However, to make full progress there must be general recognition of the fact that mental illness is a form of disease comparable to any other disease which affects the human body.
Later on, when the bill itself came up, Dr. Blair made this further statement, as recorded on page 3100 of the same volume, that is to say for April 4 of the same year:
I point out to you, sir, that we have a problem in mental disease in Canada that we will have to cope with some place somehow. I do not like the fact that mental disease is not recognized because I feel it is a backward step. It is a backward step for this reason. Mental disease may occur just as you may have pneumonia or any other disease in the categories of diseases that are treated in hospitals at the present time.
I am sorry that, some place in this bill, the minister cannot go a step farther and give further financial help to the mental hospitals. It would be of great assistance.
Perhaps some of my friends opposite will say: "Why did you not include them in the bill?" Once again, it is not a question of harking back to what we have done in the past. The fact that we did pass this bill on hospital insurance is in itself a great asset to the Liberal party. If we made a mistake- assuming that it was a mistake-in failing to include sanitaria and mental health institutions, it should be remembered that the Conservative members, headed by the present

Prime Minister, promised to correct the situation. I think that is the point on which we ought to concentrate now.
The present Minister of Finance had even gone much further in the debate. He had gone so far as to move an amendment which I wish to draw to the attention of the house. It is found on page 3380 of Hansard for 1957, volume III, and I quote:
The limitation of which I wish to speak briefly now-
I am quoting the present Minister of Finance, who was then sitting in the opposition.

is in my submission a most unfortunate limitation. I refer in particular to the express exclusion from this bill and from the scheme for which it provides of patients-whether in-patients or out-patients-in tuberculosis hospitals or sanitaria and in hospitals or institutions for the mentally ill.
From the time this government proposal was first introduced these patients enjoying either inpatient or out-patient services of such institutions have been excluded from any benefit under the scheme. We as a party and as Her Majesty's loyal opposition-
This is still the present Minister of Finance speaking:
-have already expressed in the strongest terms our view that there is no justification whatever for the exclusion of these hospitals and institutions from among those that lie within the scope of the scheme of hospital insurance.
A little farther down, on the same page, the present Minister of Finance said:
Does the house adequately realize that if these exclusions are permitted it means that the house is drawing a clear line of distinction between certain types of illness. It means that if patients are suffering from what are called physical ailments and go to hospitals they will fall within the scope of the scheme of this bill. However, if they are suffering from tuberculosis and go to hospitals provided for patients so suffering they will not fall within the scope of the bill. Similarly, in the case of patients suffering from mental illness, if they go to hospitals or institutions designed for the purpose of providing care for such patients then they lie outside the scope of the bill. No scheme which tries to draw a line of distinction between institutions of the kinds of which we are speaking, where the attempted distinction is based upon the type of illness, could possibly be sound.
And he added, page 3381:
The minister knows very well and the whole government knows that if it were not for the exclusion of institutions providing hospital care for tubercular patients and mentally ill patients more provinces would have found the proposal much more attractive than the present and undoubtedly the majority of the provincial governments would have indicated their adherence to the plan if it had been on a wider basis.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I pause for a digression. I believe the argument made at that time by the hon. member for Eglinton, who is now Minister of Finance, is altogether fallacious, because a majority of the provinces have joined the hospital insurance program without the inclusion of institutions for the mentally ill and of sanitaria.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) speaking to this motion and I am sorry he is not now in the house because I should like to make some observations on what he said and also on what he did not say.
I should first like to draw the attention of the house to motion No. 10 which, in essence, is a motion proposing that the dominion government should provide a study and funds to support a comprehensive national health insurance system in Canada with particular reference to two points; (a) the inclusion of benefits on behalf of patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and patients confined to mental institutions under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act; and (b) the introduction of legislation to provide medical, dental and optical insurance.
While I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Timiskaming I am not aware that he said anything about point (a) and it is now left open-
Mr. Speaker, may I interrupt myself to say to the hon. member for Essex East that if he would listen he might learn something. The hon. gentleman who was former minister of national health and welfare will have ample opportunity later to lecture his backbenchers but this is not the time.
If I may now continue without competition from the hon. member for Essex East I should like to comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) who dealt at some length with the matter of the inclusion of benefits for patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and patients in mental institutions. I believe there is a very sound and justifiable reason as to why this has not been done up to now and while it may be considered advantageous to include them in the future I should like at this time to bring to

the attention of the house an argument which I have not as yet heard dealt with here.
There is a great fear on the part of the provinces generally, and particularly certain people in provinces, that action taken by this house should not tend to overcentralize things that come within the ambit of property and civil rights, since they guard those rights assiduously and over which they have a particular measure of control. Therefore, I should like to point out what I am sure most hon. members know, namely that tuberculosis is a communicable disease and as such comes within the purview of the administration of provincial governments, as far as the provinces are concerned, and inmates of mental institutions are there by commitment of the provincial courts. This does not mean that those patients are bereft of benefits in respect of hospitalization, not at all. These types of patients who are treated in an active treatment hospital, either as a participating psychiatric case under the open-door policy, a day clinic, or a tuberculosis patient, are hospitalized and surgery is undertaken when it is needed in a public general hospital, or other treatment which comes under the normal provision of this act and therefore they have the full benefits of this act with its contribution by the dominion treasury.
But where it is not specified in particular is the instance of sanitaria or mental institutions. These are institutions which are the direct responsibility of the provincial governments with, I think, good and sufficient reason, because this has to do with the matter of property and civil rights. I do not want to stand on that alone, but all of these plans really have three particular aspects: one is service, one is administration and the other is the matter of finance. Both service and administration are kept as close to the matter of finance as possible. I think this is a principle of all good government and therefore when this responsibility is aligned clearly with provincial administration it seems to me that until such time as it can be shown that it can be better dealt with under another level of government it should remain where it is. This is not to say that financial consideration should not be given to those problems of the provinces by the dominion treasury in support of patients of this sort. It should.
I do maintain that with the rate of tuberculosis mortality going down and taking into consideration the care which is now being given to the mentally ill that the long stay or custodial care which tuberculosis sanitaria gave to patients in the past and care which was given in mental institutions is not as likely to be as prevalent in the future as it has been in the past. I simply point this out.
Health Insurance
At the moment I personally see no reason why this should not be as it is and in an evolutionary way the provinces could prepare to give up this responsibility if they wish to do so and the other additional financial provision which I understand is now made under the dominion-provincial agreements could meet this present situation. I do not want any member of this house or any member of the public to fear that because this type of patient is not included in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act they are not receiving financial assistance from the provinces in which they reside or are institutionalized.
Let me pass on to the (b) part of this resolution to provide medical, dental and optical insurance. With regard to optical insurance I must say that in this instance blinkers have been held over the house in taking a good look at this proposal, and this is not a proposal that we can afford to look at with blinkers because it is essentially a proposal for the dominion treasury to finance in large part the cost of a program within the provinces over which they may have little or no control, without being able to evaluate the good results which may accrue or to correct the bad results which might come from its overuse. I come back to my same premise, that any of these health measures must be looked at in the field of service, in the field of administration, and in the field of finance.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Timiskaming confused the issue in some of his assertions because he did not seem to be quite clear in his own mind exactly what public health was or the limit of the extent of hospitalization or really the content of medical care, because these three are the elements which make up any health plan on a generalized basis. I would like to avoid the word "insurance" in this connection because these things are not actuarially sound nor can they be made actuarially sound. The program of the United Kingdom is known as the national health service or the national health plan. In my opinion to mislabel it as insurance is to mislead those people who have to pay for it.
The other thing in which the hon. member for Timiskaming is confused about is the word "free". None of this service is free. The services may be provided, such as they are, at low initial cost to the consumer, if you like, but the lower the cost to the consumer it appears the higher the cost to the consolidated revenue fund. There is no control; there is no measure of evaluation, and this is why the United Kingdom from the beginning had trouble with the pharmaceutical preparations of one kind and another, such as cough mixtures and aspirin tablets.

Health Insurance
can the provinces undertake these responsibilities which are their own. In any of these schemes we must remember that you cannot require another level of government to undertake something and then say, "All right; we will pay part and you pay the rest". This is exactly what broke down the 1944-45 proposals on health insurance because the plan as then submitted by the then government was impossible of implementation in the province at the level of financing they would supply. It was not so much a lack of desire to do it as it was an impossible situation to meet in terms of cost, in terms of available personnel and in terms of administration. Nobody knew the cost and nobody was prepared to underwrite it until more information and more experience were obtained.
So I come back to the public health program with which my hon. friend had a great deal to do because it meant that one could deal in a province with the creation of what is known as a health unit. A health unit is nothing more nor less than a larger municipal unit of public health administration. In other words, in a city you have enough population to employ qualified, fulltime staff. In small urban and rural municipalities, while you need a full-time program of good content you cannot afford to employ the necessary staff full-time to do that at a strictly municipal level. Therefore by merging several municipalities, as in a county or as in several portions of a county or 'as in certain townships, a larger unit of public health administration can be created and the program for this then instituted on a full-time basis and paid for in part by the taxes of this unit on the basis of equalized assessment.
But because communicable disease is no respecter of municipal boundaries, it therefore becomes important to a province as a whole to aid by subsidy in the setting up of satisfactory programs. Therefore practically everywhere in Canada of which I know these health units or larger units of public health administration are subsidized in part by the provincial government which hopes in one way or another to obtain financial relief from the dominion treasury. This provides a full-time medical officer of health, full-time nursing personnel, full-time sanitary inspectors with transportation, offices and what-not, to be able to bring to even outlying rural municipalities those services in preventive medicine which are the reasons that our birth rate has been maintained with the drop in infant mortality, why there is this longer expectation of life at birth now than we have ever known

before and why in general the control of communicable disease has now been achieved wherever we can get people to pay attention.
These are the only two mandatory things in a public health program, namely control of communicable disease and the control of nuisances which boils down to a matter of sanitation, both environmental and communal. These are the only two mandatory things in a public health program. But when it comes to immunization, unless you have an understanding on the part of the public and their willingness to subscribe to an immunization program, you do not get anywhere. Prior to the development of Salk vaccine and its use here and elsewhere, the great cry of course was this: why does not the medical profession develop a vaccine which will rid us of this great scourge? You had all this going on and we all hoped it would come and eventually it did come. On the introduction of Salk vaccine great care had to be taken to prevent from getting it people who were anxious to obtain this vaccine, who were prepared to pay large sums of money to get it ahead of others; in other words, there was a danger of bootlegging Salk vaccine.
These measures of control-and my friend the hon. member for Essex East had a hand in it and it was very well done-meant that Salk vaccine could be reserved for that level of age group in the population which was most susceptible to poliomyelitis and which should have had it first. Now a few years after the introduction of Salk vaccine, we are obliged to go on television and radio in order to get parents to bring their children in to complete the course in this immunizing program. Hence I say that the matter of the education of the public, the understanding of the public, is one of the most essential things in any health scheme. We do it in terms of public health. We do it in terms of medical care. I think this is one of the problems in a medical care program.
For instance, we have seen the rise of programs in the name of preventive medicine that are programs of health supervision for groups of people. These are called group hygiene programs, if you will. There is the matter of the expectant mother and her child, the so-called maternal and infant programs; the school child which goes from school age to the adolescent period in the high school; and what was formerly the industrial but now is the occupational program. The possibilities for these health supervision programs lie in the fact that you are dealing with groups of people of relatively similar age who have a task in common. In other words, the pregnant woman has a task in producing live young.

The school child is there because it is receiving an education; and the worker in industry or other occupation has a task to perform and many of their problems are common to the group as a whole.
My friend the hon. member for Timiskam-ing talked in terms of weak eyes, bad teeth and other things which he hoped would be corrected late in life through a medical care plan. That is not the time to correct them. They should not exist. The time to correct them is through the instruction which is given to the expectant mother, by the understanding of her own care, the care of her newborn child and the care in the raising of this child into the school age group. I must say the women of Canada are doing extraordinarily well in raising their children because when they come into the first grade now all over the country they are healthy, bright, able specimens. Then the school program picks up with the supervision of the school medical officer, the civic nurse and where this much does not exist, it is the fault of the province or the municipality in which that school resides. It is no fault of anybody else but the local community because there is money available for it.
There has been publicity as to its value and if people will not take advantage of these things which are there in the name of the province I do not know how you are going to institute a program of cure by care or care for cure that will achieve the same result at so little cost. Therefore continued publicity, continued education in the value of these measures at these group levels is a most important field and the Department of National Health and Welfare is doing this with considerable success.
In the occupational field-and I come back to the hon. member for Timiskaming; I think anybody who has worked in a plant has had experience with it-formerly there was some sort of provision for medical care. The aspirin, cough syrup and sulphur and molasses type of treatment it hinged upon has now been displaced-and I think fairly thoroughly displaced-by thoroughly appreciated programs of initial periodic medical examination, the availability of advice from physicians and nurses within the plant, the opportunity to assist people to help themselves.
This is one of the most important single contributions that anyone can make to the health of a population, namely to help people to help themselves. No doctor or anyone else can do it for them. It is something that rests essentially with the individual and only that individual can do it as far as that individual can go himself, at which time he must have
Health Insurance
additional support, advice and skilled care. But the educational program through use in our occupational and medical program is having great value; with its medical examination at periodic intervals, taking into account the age and sex of the individual; having an appreciation of the individual as an individual, not as a number on a chart, not as something which is legislated into the necessity of having a medical examination but rather as something which is available to them and which in time they appreciate. Many of these things in their origin were difficult to establish because people had this natural fear that any medical plan in a plant, office or store was designed to seek ways and means of eliminating them from their jobs on excuses of ill health when, in fact, it was for some other reason.
This has been overcome, and I would say from my own personal experience and experience with associates that this matter of the periodic medical examination of the adult group is doing more to reduce the severity of those disabling conditions which are noninfectious, the cardio vascular diseases and malignancies. It is doing more to reduce their severity by the earlier discovery of their existence before the individual has noticed sufficiently to visit the doctor to find out what is his trouble.
In the case of cancer particularly we have gone a great distance to break down the fear, particularly in women, of a visit to the doctor in case cancer would be discovered. In other words, as part of the periodic medical examination, perhaps once a year or once in eighteen months, they would go through this routine. They have learned to do this. They are not afraid to have this examination, and if by chance-and it is not often-some early untoward sign or symptom is discovered, then these people have the opportunity of seeking further and skilled medical advice to pursue this early sign or symptom in the hope, of course, that the diagnosis will not be malignant cancer.
As a comfort to those who have to be told that there is a problem, of those which are sent for further investigation of malignancy arising out of the early sign or symptom, a very high percentage do not have cancer. Of the very small percentage of those-it is less than one half of one per cent-which have symptoms which are or could be cancer, which of course relates to the particular group, the 45-68 group, only a small percentage are found to have a definite malignancy which needs immediate surgical care. Our surgical care is such at the moment

Health Insurance
that we are finding that the period of expectancy of active, healthy life after operation has been extended from five to ten, and now to fifteen years longer. So many of these people in the older age group end out their days and die from something else, not from the cancer of which they were afraid.
Mr. Speaker, other speakers have emphasized the role voluntary services have played and all the things which have happened to raise the standard of medical care in Canada. I would like to say that I agree with anyone who says that the standard of medical care here is the best in the world.
I believe it. I have seen most of the other countries which have standard medical care, but I believe that our present interns and the people who come from our medical schools have skill, ethics and ability which are second to none. I think that is borne out by the number of people we receive from abroad who come to lecture on visiting professorships and spend some time here. I know this because I am one of the examiners periodically for the medical council of Canada and I have people who sit with me occasionally who are astonished at the skill and knowledge of our graduates.
I hope that this trend which is certainly interfering with recruitment of people from medical schools for one reason or another is reversed, because Canada needs more doctors not fewer. Until we have more doctors this question of equitable distribution is a difficult one. Medicine is so specialized today that the services of highly technical laboratories, expensive apparatus, and so on, has to be concentrated largely in urban centres. It must of necessity. Therefore you have a higher percentage of specialists in urban, particularly university centres than otherwise.
This is particularly so with the system of medicine as now practised in our children's hospitals. I could give you as one example the hospital for sick children in Toronto, which is not just a Toronto hospital but a province of Ontario hospital with an outstanding and nationwide record, with the rest of the province of Ontario channelling their children into it. This is what is happening all over the country. You cannot create artificial drainage areas of trade. You cannot create artificial areas for supply in medicine or in anything else. Therefore this has to be something which is natural, which has grown and is liked and respected and can be supported. That would be my fear, the participation of-let us call it quite plainly-a state medical care plan upon a relatively unsuspecting public at heaven knows what cost, when if we look at what we have, which is good, and tidy up those things which are the

main things of which people complain, we have sufficient care provided at this time.
What are these main things of which people complain? They complain, first of all, that it is difficult to get a doctor. That may be so. On the other hand, this is not always the fault of the doctor in the community. It may also to some extent be the fault of the patient, who could call at seven in the evening instead of midnight, who could have come into his office the day before. A doctor on an average looks after some two thousand patients and just cannot work round the clock. With consideration from the public the problems of the medical profession would be helped.
This is also true in pioneering areas, for example, where you may have no physician at all. I think I can tell hon. members of this because it was an extraordinary situation. One section of the United States with the lowest morbidity and mortality rate and with a comparable population with other states was an area where they had not had a doctor for ten years. Of course, I do not want that to be a reflection generally on the medical profession, but that is true, and therefore without a doctor perhaps one might take more care and consider those things which should be avoided because one would know that there was difficulty in obtaining help.
Again, I do not want to be facetious about this but let me go back to Saskatchewan once more. The hon. member admitted there was a lot of good in Saskatchewan. I suggest that the system of aeroplane service and the flying ambulance service which was instituted there and elsewhere could be organized by provincial administrations. I am sorry to see the hon. member is not in the house because he might have learned something about this.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the house; I have very little more to say. However, I would like to say that this was the average cost in Ontario at that particular time.
Costs since that time have sky-rocketed. They have sky-rocketed because the price of labour, the price of food, the price of everything which goes into a hospital has gone up to the point that the average charge per day is now somewhere around $15, $16, or even more. This is not something with which we can quarrel. This is something which we have to meet. It is important on the part of hospital administration that they do not think they have a blank cheque to cash every time they want more money for services which they render. They have a responsibility to continue to provide good service at the lowest possible cost to the public treasury.
It seems to me that some consideration will have to be given to the number of patients in hospitals who are there for more than 30 days, because it has been shown that the transference of such patients from the active general hospital to convalescent institutions of a rehabilitation type which might be situated in a wing of the hospital or in the same grounds would reduce the average days stay per patient so subtantially that it would be possible in a year or two to build a new hospital unit with the money saved. This is an established fact.
We have all been impressed, and, I think, hurt, by the stories-and we all know of them-of people whose life savings have vanished and to whom great hardship has been caused by reason of these difficult and long illnesses. These cases are not numerous in terms of the total load of illness, but they seem to occur at the least convenient times and usually to the people who least expect it and can least afford it. It may therefore be desirable to provide for a further extension of insurance of a disaster type, partly or even wholly under government auspices, so as to prevent a family's savings being wiped out by the tremendous cost of these long enduring illnesses.
In addition, there is the continuing and pressing problem of outpatient hospital services. The wise use of hospital outpatient facilities is, in itself, a most important part of the field of preventive medicine. For years these departments were run as clinics, and the loss sustained by most hospitals with respect to their outpatient departments represented the total loss for the year. This is 79951-0-98
Health Insurance
particularly true with regard to the city of Montreal. The loss in this department in the Montreal general hospital which has had a fine record in the community for over 100 years, has been fantastic as a result of maintaining these services to the community.
Thus, apart from the interest I have in the province of Ontario, I express the hope that at some good time those responsible for the administration of Quebec will see fit to implement a hospital insurance plan in keeping with the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, and that the hospitals themselves, in co-operation with the medical profession, will enable us to find a way to improve and assist the work of hospital outpatient departments which, I believe, is one of the best single means of keeping people reasonably well and discovering and treating difficulties before more serious illness results, thus extending the happiness and longevity of our people.

In making the few brief remarks which I had intended to make on this resolution, I must first of all apologize for not being in a position to compete with the knowledge and experience in this particular field of the two hon. members on the government side who have so far taken part in this debate. Both are medical practitioners and have had ample opportunity to familiarize themselves with this subject, particularly the aspect now under discussion.
I must say that it is the duty of parliament not only to introduce new legislation but also to amend and approve existing legislation. We must admit that no legislation is perfect, and it should be improved if possible after it has been observed in operation for a period of time. This applies to the hospital insurance plan which was introduced by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) in April, 1957. The hospital insurance act, or the health insurance act, is only one of the many social security measures which were introduced by the Liberal administration and which are enjoyed today by the entire population of Canada.
The present resolution introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) calls for the introduction of a comprehensive system of national health insurance, and, more particularly, to give consideration to the following:
(a) Amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to provide benefits on behalf of patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and patients confined to mental institutions; (b) introducing legislation to provide medical, dental and optical insurance.
The hon. member who has just resumed his seat attempted to show good and justifiable reason why this has not been done, why

Health Insurance
tuberculosis and mental disorders have not been included in the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. I would have liked to have heard the hon. member say why, if such reasons exist today, they did not exist in 1957. I should also have liked to have asked him to explain, if he could, the position taken then by hon. members of the opposition of that day and particularly by the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) and the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) as well as by the late hon. member for Lanark, Mr. Blair. It is the responsibility of members of the present government to implement by positive and concrete action the promises which they made to the electors of this country, and to put into effect now the things they were advocating when they sat on the opposition side of this house.
Many of those who are now members of the present government took part in the debate which took place in April, 1957 when the health insurance bill was introduced. Those of us who were here at that time will recall the remarks made on that occasion by such hon. members as the hon. member for Prince Albert, the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). All these gentlemen are today members of the government, and it is interesting to hear what they have to say with regard to the measures which they were advocating less than three years ago. They have had ample opportunity to implement those very same measures. What have they done about it? Was it not the hon. member for Eglinton, now the Minister of Finance, who moved on April 10, 1957:
-that Bill 320 be not now read the third time but that the said bill be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering clause 2 subsection (e) thereof.
In explaining the purpose of his motion the hon. member called to the attention of the house the financial difficulties experienced by the provinces and municipalities of this country and insisted on the elimination, to use his own words, of the unworthy distinction in the definition of hospitals to be covered by the act. If the clause then referred to was unworthy of the Canadian parliament, to use the minister's own words as recorded at page 3382 of Hansard for April 10, 1957, the hon. minister should listen to his own conscience and practise now what he was preaching when he addressed the house on that date. The financial difficulties of the provinces and municipalities are just as severe today and if not worse than they were in 1957. What about a municipality which must borrow at 7 or 7J per cent as compared with interest rates in the vicinity of 5 per cent as they were in 1957?
[Mr. Eoblchaud.l
What about the hon. member for Prince Albert? What did he have to say on the occasion to which I referred? As Prime Minister of this country can he now question the omission which he could not see in 1957 when sitting on the opposition side of this house? Has he now found a serious reason as to why tuberculosis and mental hospitals should not be included in the hospital insurance scheme? Why is he now taking an attitude so different from the one he took in 1957 when he made the statement which was placed on the record earlier in this debate by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard)? I shall again place that statement on the record. The Prime Minister said, as reported at page 3386 of Hansard of April 10, 1957:
I say that the legislation in its present form is discriminatory in that it denies these institutions a right that should be theirs.
The hon. gentleman was referring at that time to tuberculosis and mental institutions.
The hon. member for Timiskaming in the second part of his resolution calls for the consideration of the introduction of legislation to provide medical, dental and optical insurance. The Liberal party's policy favours the implementation of health insurance provisions against major medical and surgical expenses which, combined with hospital insurance, would ensure that no Canadian would be financially crippled by illness. Such a policy, I am convinced, could be implemented in co-operation with the provinces and each individual concerned. I am therefore of the opinion that this part of the resolution dealing with medical, dental and optical care should also receive very careful consideration.
At this point I must admit, however, that we should perhaps make certain reservations. I feel that such provisions should be carefully looked into before being put into effect so as to avoid as much as possible the introduction of abuses and also to ascertain the availability of practitioners in adequate numbers to take care of cases without possible discrimination.
The experience gained from the application of the present hospital insurance plan could be of great value in the introduction of a health insurance program. Most of us are fully aware of the problems created by the shortage of hospital beds in those provinces where the hospital insurance scheme has been introduced. The problem is aggravated by the almost impossible position of municipalities, religious congregations or other groups in terms of financing new hospitals or even additions to existing facilities.
We must admit there is a shortage of hospital beds and the situation is becoming

more serious every day as the hospital insurance scheme is being taken advantage of by a larger number of patients. How can we expect, for example, a religious order to undertake the construction of a new hospital or even an addition to an existing one if the interest and depreciation charges cannot be included in the per diem rate charged hospital patients? Can municipalities be expected to contribute further to hospitals when their sources of taxation have been exhausted and the present rates of interest have reached an all time high?
Let us take for an example the conditions in my own province of New Brunswick or even my own constituency of Gloucester. In Gloucester county today there is a shortage of from 200 to 250 hospital beds. How can we expect religious orders to proceed with new construction unless they have an assurance with respect to depreciation and interest rates. Our municipal taxes are about the highest in Canada and any further increase would force existing industries to close their doors. Something must be done in order to provide additional hospital beds. This can be made possible only by including interest rates and depreciation in the existing hospital insurance scheme. I would urge the government to reconsider this most important aspect of the hospital insurance plan. I would suggest that this is just as important and urgent as the suggestion included in the resolution presently under discussion.
The present Minister of Justice must recall his intervention with respect to this matter in the debate on April 4, 1957. If he was convinced then that depreciation costs and interest should be included in the scheme he must be in a better position today to convince the government of which he is a member of the need for implementing at this time the suggestions he was advocating when the legislation was introduced in this house. This was a promise and a commitment made inside and outside the house by hon. members of the government and we are anxious to see what will be the attitude of the government on this particular aspect of the hospital insurance program.
