Mr. Speaker, I too, should like to make a few brief remarks with regard to the resolution we have been discussing today. We have heard various hon. members in the house give us their views with regard to the question embodied in the resolution. The resolution, of course, has two distinct parts, the first relating to the inclusion of tuberculosis sanitaria and mental institutions under 79951-0-981
Health Insurance
the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the second relating to the introduction of legislation to provide medical, dental and optical insurance.
It is my opinion that the time has not yet come when these matters should be implemented. Certainly the problems of tuberculosis and mental health are of extreme importance in Canada. As we all know, tuberculosis is gradually declining and some of the facilities built in Canada in past years for this purpose are now empty. Mental health is one of the most important special medical problems in Canada and in this field we are also witnessing a change in concept of treatment. We are turning from the concept of treatment in large institutions to the type of treatment associated with the so-called open-door policy, community planning and the prevention of mental illness. This subject was capably outlined by my colleague the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian). In my opinion it would not be appropriate at this time to include tuberculosis and mental hospitals in the national hospital scheme.
Just for the record let me say that in 1957 only 2 per cent of the revenue of tuberculosis hospitals and 9 per cent of the revenue of mental hospitals was derived from self-paying patients. In other words, it could be considered that it is well within the financial resources of the provinces to completely cover these services.
The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robi-chaud) says that the provinces are no better off as a result of this scheme. The province of Alberta is certainly better off because of the receipt of funds from the federal government under the hospital insurance plan. Unfortunately, the government of Alberta chose to replace the funds it had been using for hospitals with federal funds and therefore the municipalities must continue to carry a considerable load. Certainly, psychiatric units in general hospitals are now covered and, as the hon. member for Durham pointed out, active surgical treatment of tuberculosis patients is also covered.
Then we come to the more thorny problem of part (b) of the resolution with regard to the very sweeping generalization of medical, dental and optical insurance. First of all, may I say that the hon. member who introduced the resolution probably introduced it mostly for political purposes; for he failed to stay in the house and listen to the arguments presented, particularly that of the hon. member for Durham. His whole attitude toward the idea of medical insurance seemed to be political. May I clear up my position immediately. I am in favour of a plan which

Health Insurance
in co-operation with the provinces will give the people the maximum amount of service and yet will be a plan of freedom, freedom for the patient and freedom for the doctor.
I should like to consider the British health scheme which was mentioned by the hon. member for Timiskaming. First of all, it is very difficult indeed to compare the system, usage and medical practice in Britain with that to which we are accustomed in Canada. He says the United Kingdom scheme is good and everybody is happy with it. I have a quotation here which does not seem to bear that out. It is a quotation from Hansard of 1954, by the late Dr. Blair who was quoting one of the eminent physicians in the old country with regard to his opinion of the health scheme in England at that time. I am quoting from page 6298 of Hansard of June 19, 1954:
Dr. Hale-White listed four complaints against the medical scheme, which has been in effect since 1948.
They were:
1. The introduction of the scheme led to the belittling of the general practitioner, because the government stressed that the public would have access to the best specialists under socialized medicine.
Here we come to another problem. In England at the present time the standard of medical practice as undertaken by the general practitioner is nowhere near the standard that we have in Canada in general practice. This has been brought about specifically by the introduction of their socialized state medicine. This is not something which we in Canada can afford to do today, for the standard of care which we want in our system of medicine in Canada has been based on-and I hope very strongly it will continue to be based on-the strong position of the general practitioner in both urban and rural areas.
The second complaint that he had with this scheme in effect in the old country was that:
People began bothering the doctors and hospitals with trivial matters.
As a practising physician I say that this is an important matter and it has already come to our attention with regard to hospitalization schemes. We are now being asked to put people into hospital for a rest; we are asked to put people in hospital so that they can get away from some stresses and strains that they are running into in their ordinary life, and it becomes very difficult for the doctor to do anything about this, and it can become particularly serious under a state system of medicine.
I understand, as the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) pointed out, it has got down to the point where to get

extra income which these poor chaps in general practice in England have, they have to get down to giving out certificates so that people may miss work and attend football games and the like. This could happen here. It used to happen in the days of prohibition when doctors were writing prescriptions for alcohol. The doctor's time was taken up in writing prescriptions and he never saw patients. This was not practising medicine. This is not what we want in Canada.
Third, the incentive for the doctor to give good care was not there under the state system which was in effect in England. The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has gone over that and has pointed out that this incentive would be lost; that we who are in the practice of medicine are not in it only for the income but for other intangibles, if you like, and also the idea of serving the people, not as wards of the state or civil servants but as free men willing to practise as we wish. This is our incentive. We take post-graduate work. This is our incentive, to increase our knowledge; this is our incentive, to give our patients the best possible care, and this cannot be accomplished under any statism sort of medical practice.
As I said, I am personally in favour of some sort of plan but I do not believe that we in Canada are ready for that plan yet. If we take a look at sickness or illness we will find that there are several components. Several things happen when somebody gets sick. It is not just a question of going to the doctor. There may be the question of hospitalization; there may be the question of buying drugs. There may be the question of loss of income of the breadwinner, and this is the question I want to deal with for a moment. Certainly in Canada, now that we have a national hospital scheme-we were all very happy to see this come in and we are very pleased that this government brought in the scheme-we have to look at what is the next big cost to the patient or to the patient's family at any time that illness strikes. I would suggest that the next big cost to these people is the loss of income. Perhaps we should give further consideration to this; perhaps it has priority over just the cost of medical services alone.
There are other things we have to do in Canada before we are ready for a generalized system of free comprehensive medical care. First of all, the hospitalization scheme has shown the need for more hospital beds and here I might say that I feel we should work along the lines not necessarily of bigger hospitals but perhaps more hospitals generally. I feel very strongly that we could

economize on our hospital construction; we could economize on hospital care if we were to come forward with a system of cottage hospitals surrounding large urban areas, and get away from those massive institutions of
1,000	beds and more. It seems to me it is something like corporate enterprise. Once you get so big you start to run into overhead; you start to run into other problems which come from bigness alone. We perhaps require one large centre in a large area where we can have centralized pathological and other diagnostic equipment; but certainly, for the active treatment of most people, we can do these things more economically and give better care and be more humanitarian in the care of our patients with a system of cottage hospitals surrounding some of those larger urban areas. I say this with a knowledge of what is going on in northern Alberta. I feel very strongly that a lot of the beds in those institutions, beds in research institutions are taken up by people who could very well be taken care of in beds in cottage hospitals surrounding those larger centres. Certainly, if we are going to give a comprehensive medical care plan to our people besides hospitals we need personnel.
My hon. friends have pointed out this afternoon that registrations in medical schools across Canada are going down. I believe that one of the reasons they are going down is this statism which has been talked about and which people are afraid is going to be brought into the field of medicine. Doctors are a little bit like farmers. They are individualists and they want to stay that way. They want to be able to practise medicine in their own way, using the best methods that can be devised.
If we are going to have a comprehensive health scheme we are certainly going to need other types of personnel that we do not have now and that are not in training now. I refer to mental health people who would be involved in social work in the mental health field and psychologists and psychiatrists. The number of people entering these fields for training at the moment is not what it was even a few years ago. Surely before we commit our country to a national health scheme it is sound to continue our training grants along these lines so we will have more mental health personnel and all the other technicians that would be required as part of a comprehensive health scheme.
Another great part of medical practice which must be given some consideration and discussion is the question of nursing personnel. In this field things are evolving but certainly they have to evolve more so that we
Health Insurance
will have a greater number of nursing personnel and more adequate standards. Over the past few years we have seen the development of the use of ward aids or nurses' assistants. I think this is a good thing but certainly we still have to have our nurse executives, the people who run the show in the hospitals. These are the people who will be doing the actual nursing and administering the regulations. We have to give consideration to the training of more personnel if we are going to cover all our people under a comprehensive scheme.
Basically, the point is that now is not the time for a national health plan. We must work on all these other things and bring them up to a standard where they will fit into a national health scheme. Throughout the country there are various voluntary associations formed by interested people, some of them sponsored by groups or provincial associations of medical practitioners. These associations are doing a good job. In a discussion of this kind it might be worth while to consider whether or not, they could not do a better job with government assistance, and provide comprehensive coverage for all the people within their areas. This is the type of system which I should like to see brought in because it would leave that freedom which is so vital to a country like Canada. We have to do this groundwork first.
I was going to mention public health and I only do so to reinforce the argument of the hon. member for Durham in which he so capably outlined the possibilities and necessities in that particular field.
I have mentioned some of the things that I believe should be done before we have a national health scheme. Again, if it is at all possible I would ask the C.C.F. party to keep this sort of thing out of politics. This is not something that should be used as a political club in the way that they have tried to use it. This is not something that they should use as a plank to weep over in their platforms. They are dealing with people, with their illnesses and their health. Health is so often a matter of attitude and concept, and these are things which socialism never takes into consideration. To my mind that is why socialized medicine can never enhance the general health of the country to any great degree at all because if you do not have freedom in this as in other things your general level is going to fall.
Again I say that if any national scheme is put into effect in Canada I hope we will consider the basis on which medical practice is now carried on in Canada. The basis has to be the general practitioner and he must be preserved at all costs because he is of

Health Insurance
great value to the general health of the country. In England he has not progressed with the rest of the medical profession because he has not had the opportunity to do so. He is restricted from practising in the larger hospitals. Only lately has there been talk of cottage hospitals in which the general practitioner can practise. These are important things. If you tend to take incentive away from these people who are the backbone of the medical profession then your scheme will not be very good for the health of the people of the country.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard three members from the government side of the house speak in this debate today. All three are also members of the medical profession and, as a result, should be men who are well qualified to speak on this subject before us today. Unfortunately I missed part of the speech of the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian); but from what I heard of it, I thought he made an excellent speech; and I am referring particularly to the last part of it.
However, I am afraid I cannot extend the same congratulations with regard to the speeches made by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) and the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner). In fact, I thought that the hon. member for Jasper-Edson did not measure up to his usual standard in the inference he made about the mover of this motion, when he referred to the fact that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) was not in this house at the time. I should like to say that if the hon. member for Jasper-Edson devotes to his job the same amount of time as does the hon. member for Timiskaming and if he serves his constituents as well, he can face them in the next election with a clear conscience.
I listened carefully to the speech made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson and I must say I found it extremely difficult to follow the line of reasoning throughout his speech. He was against this proposal, he was for it and, above all, according to him, we must wait until everything else is in shape before we can hope for a national health insurance plan in this country. He also with great

regularity brought in the old, frayed-edged cliches about regimentation, state medicine and control, lack of freedom and all the rest of it.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa also proceeded to impute motives to the hon. member for Timiskaming, implying that the only interest he had in this particular resolution was a political one and not anything else; that it was not meant to assist the health of people of Canada but was meant to place people in a mould, to regiment them and all that sort of thing. To me it seems strange that both hon. members, while insisting that we should keep this matter out of politics, proceeded to give, in my opinion, a political diatribe instead of a constructive speech on this subject. They both also made a great effort to try to create the picture that doctors are flocking out of the United Kingdom to get away from regimentation under the national health insurance plan in Great Britain.
I should like to look into the facts with regard to this allegation. I have here in my hand a copy of The Lancet which I believe is a weekly medical journal published in Great Britain. This one is for the week of Saturday, November 23, 1957. It deals with this very matter raised by the hon. members today with regard to the flocking of British doctors to get away from this regimentation. At page 1043, where it is dealing with a report of a committee to study this particular subject, I find this:
But they believe that continuation of the present increase of students would yield after 1961 more doctors than are likely to be needed and a reduction of the present intake by about one tenth as soon as practicable would be wise.
I fail to see any resemblance between this report and the picture these two hon. members tried to create in this house today. Then again at page 1058 we find something else which deals with some allegations made by the hon. members or at least with the picture they tried to create, namely that doctors were flocking out of Great Britain. At that page I find this:
The committee estimate that the present number of doctors from Great Britain who leave to settle and practise overseas (including medical missionaries) is just under 400 per annum. The present number of doctors from overseas ... who settle and practise in this country is just over 200 per annum. There is thus a current net export of just under 200 doctors per annum.
That figure is out of a total count, as of 1955, of 53,260 doctors in Britain which means that they have 0.3 per cent of the doctors in Britain leaving to get away from this terrible regimentation we hear so much

about. I do not know what is the percentage of doctors leaving Canada but I am willing to bet that it is in excess of 0.3 per cent.
We also heard that since this plan came into effect in Britain the doctors have been swamped with patients who call on them for no reason at all and that the standard of service has deteriorated rapidly year by year. We find again in the same report- and this is from the Willink report-the following at page 1057:
Between 1952 and 1955 the number of patients per doctor's list fell from 2436 to 2283 in England and Wales and from 2074 to 1975 in Scotland-
The picture which the two hon. members tried to paint in this house is not borne out by the facts.
They also expressed grave alarm about young people in this country not going into the medical field and they said this was due to fear of this terrible regimentation which was hanging over their heads. I would say that the only fear is in the minds of those two hon. gentlemen and other hon. gentlemen who base their opinions on prejudice rather than on facts. If we look again at page 1043 of this publication we find the following:
When the national health service was started, fears were expressed lest the quite obvious underdoctoring of the country should lead politicians to insist that medical schools should step up their production, even though for a time they had to lower standards. These fears were not realized: though the schools increased their intake, they did so chiefly because more young men and women (including many from the forces) wanted to be trained.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) listed some figures compiled from various service organizations, and so on and so forth, which are supposed to look after all the ills of this country. If I recall rightly, and I have to recall from memory because I have not seen the report of his remarks, he said that since 1942 there had been something like $260 million spent in this field. I would like to point out that that is just twice the amount that has been spent since 1948 to service the sick gold' industry, and when we look at the health of all the people in Canada, I think they deserve better treatment than that.
Another thing I would like to deal with very briefly is a subject which has been raised by government members, I believe in an attempt to try and make out that the C.C.F. are recommending free medicine. I would like to make it very clear that I do not subscribe to that idea. I do not even
Health Insurance
believe in the free gifts we receive from stores today-which we have to pay for-let alone trying to tell people that they can get free medicine. You get nothing for free in this world, and if you get medicine it just has to be paid for somehow. Whether it is paid for by a premium or through your taxes, it still has to be paid for by the people who get the service.
It was not very long ago when the many hon. members of this house said the same things they are saying now about the dread of health insurance about the dread of hospital insurance. It was just as big a bogey in those days as is health insurance today. Where are those voices now? I suggest that when health insurance comes to this country, as it will come inevitably regardless of how many people try to fight it, and regardless of whatever unsound reasons they use to try to fight it, the criticisms which we hear today and the fears which we hear expressed today will be gone like a fog which disappears in the morning. I would suggest that hon. members for Portage-Neepawa and Jasper-Edson do a little more studying on this subject. They should not base their remarks on old cliches and old prejudices but should try to study this subject, look at it dispassionately and come out with facts. I suggest that if they keep on in the way they are now they will be doing a disservice both to their profession and their country as a whole.
There is only one other point I want to raise tonight because I know that many other hon. members would like to speak in this debate. It has to do with another matter covered by this resolution, and it is the implementation of some kind of dental service which is so badly needed in this country. I think the reports from dental associations show that that is one of the biggest needs in this country, a better dental service than we have at the present time. I am not saying this in criticism particularly of the dentists themselves; I am saying it in criticism of the way we have looked at the dental service which is provided and the lack of interest we have shown in it in the past. We have only to think of the terrible condition we find when our children start school because of the terrific backlog of dental attention needed by our children.
I would also like to point out that doctors and dentists, like members of parliament or any other profession in the country, have their good ones and their bad ones, and I do not think any one profession or any one group of

Health Insurance
people are all good or all bad. However, there are some dentists who can, and should bear looking into.
I recall one instance from my own experience concerning something which happened to a member of my family who was recommended to go down to a dentist in the city of Ottawa who is supposed to be one of the best in the profession, Dr. Lome Mac-Lachlan. When we went to see him we received a two-hour sales talk which would put to shame many of our top salesmen who we see on the T.V. medium today. We also discovered that this sales talk was pretty expensive because it was going to cost us something in the neighbourhood of $500 for one set of dentures plus a few extractions. He was not even going to do the work himself; this was purely for the teeth which were required. In the mixup of the dental surgery which was done we received a bill which we paid thinking it was for the work which had been done. Much to our chagrin we discovered afterwards that we had paid $60 only for the two-hour interview and we still owed the money for the work done. Finally it transpired that the bill in Ottawa for a few extractions and a little dental surgery was $120 and the bill for the balance of the extractions and the set of dentures, which work was done in the town of Timmins, amounted to another $120. As I said, I am not accusing the whole dental profession, but it seems dentists, the same as anyone else, can stand some looking into.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take undue advantage of the time provided by the house for the discussion of this matter. I therefore propose to deal as briefly as possible and without any introductory remarks with an issue that is of great interest to all Canadians; I mean hospital insurance. My chief purpose is to explain my position here as a member from the province of Quebec, and also as a practising dentist, a profession which I have been practising for many years and which gives me, in any case, some experience as well as the right to make my viewpoint known in this house.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) suggests that the benefits of the hospital insurance scheme be extended. His proposal is to allow people in sanitaria or in mental hospitals to come within the scope of the present legislation. He suggests that the act apply to people who need medical, dental and optical care. I entirely agree
[Mr. Martin (Timmins) .1
with him, but I maintain that, first of all, the hospital insurance scheme be made acceptable to all provinces in this country.
Health, as all hon. members will agree, is, according to the British North America Act, under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Provincial governments have, indeed, the right and the responsibility to determine what must be done in that field. They have the right to do so, without first obtaining the federal government's permission, whose part with regard to health and hospitalization is only to assist and second provincial legislation in this field. In this respect, I want to point out that, since the Conservatives have been in power in Ottawa, the present government has never taken the least action which would infringe upon the principles of autonomy which we, Conservatives from Quebec or from other provinces, have preached outside this house.
While discussions regarding the establishment of a hospital insurance program started at the time of the Liberals, we cannot ignore the fact that the leader of the Ontario Conservative government, the Hon. Leslie Frost, was first to launch the movement. And if I am prepared to recognize the part played in that field by the representative from Essex East (Mr. Martin), the hon. member will not hesitate to recognize that the Liberals were led into that undertaking by the premier of the government in Toronto, and that it is only fair to stress this fact.
This being said, I note that the first agreements which made the national program applicable were entered into under a Conservative administration and as a consequence of amendments introduced by the federal Conservatives. Those amendments still seemed impossible early in 1957, so that if our party had not come into office in June 1957, this generous measure would still be a mere project. On the other hand, being a member from the province of Quebec, I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I would like my constituents to share in this national program to which they contribute just as much as people in the nine other provinces. Indeed, it is impossible not to see at this time that, whenever a dollar is paid out of the federal treasury to operate the hospital insurance scheme, whether in Ontario, in British Columbia or elsewhere, 33 cents on the dollar comes from taxes paid by Quebec taxpayers, in spite of the fact that they get nothing from the federal government to pay for hospital costs in their own province.

I fully realize that the three premiers we have had in Quebec since June 1957 did not want to engage in something as important as this without giving the matter serious consideration. Besides the three Union Na-tionale premiers have clearly and frankly explained that the hospital system of the province of Quebec is different from that of the nine other provinces of Canada. Therefore, all federal members of parliament who think, as I do, that provincial autonomy is more than just a hollow byword to be flung about at election time, recognize that we, of the federal government, have no right to tell the provinces-the provincial premiers-what sound autonomy should consist of.
I believe that we must leave the provincial government absolutely free to tell us whether a joint measure such as this is acceptable or not. It is with this feeling and in line with this idea that the party to which I belong has signed agreements with nine of the ten provinces, while the Quebec legislature is discussing the possibility of establishing a hospital insurance program which will be accepted, I hope, by the central government.
I think the ministers of this government have done all they could to make the hospital insurance program acceptable by all provinces. I think that in implementing that national program, the present federal government did not want to play the role of the one who dictates what should be done, but that of an assistant, in the light of existing provincial hospital systems. It will be up to the Quebec government's ministers to determine whether the present national program is acceptable or not.
It is up to the Quebec government, and to it alone, in fact, to say whether it is left free to set up hospital insurance in Quebec, in accordance with existing legislation and hospital traditions in that province.
If the study undertaken in this respect by the Quebec government showed that federal assistance in the field of health cannot be accepted by the province of Quebec, this would mean that in all fairness we should amend our legislation so that it would be applicable to and in harmony with the Quebec legislation to enable the province which I represent in this house to get a fair share of the federal tax revenue.
Another point of great interest to me in the resolution of the hon. member for Timis-kaming has to do with insurance for medical, dental and eye care. Because you are a dentist, you will say. And I do not hesitate to answer, 79951-0-99

yes. In thirty years of dental practice, I was able, in fact, to realize that too many people are unjustly deprived of care, not only of dental care, but also of medical and eye care, because their income does not enable them to seek treatment when it is time.
All my colleagues, dentists, physicians or specialists, who are members of this house will, without hesitation, agree with me when I say that we have allowed the health of Canadians to decline because we have failed to give them the means to see the doctor, the dentist or the specialist except at the point of death in the case of general medicine; only when the most drastic treatment became imperative in the case of dental care; and Anally, only when mere relief was possible in the case of eye care.
I shall not waste the time of this house, Mr. Speaker, in trying to show how it pays dividends to practise preventive medicine. Everybody in this house, whether he be a doctor or not, knows that the majority of diseases affecting patients can be prevented or, anyway, that the ravages of most current diseases can be alleviated to a considerable extent, if the patient is cared for early enough. However, the patient must have the means of paying for the required treatment before his sickness stops him from performing his daily work and earning his living.
There is a lot of talk today of great achievements in the intellectual field, and I am happy, as a Canadian, to find that our intellectual culture is much more widespread today than it was 25, 30, 40 or 50 years ago. I am very pleased about it, but still I think that physical health remains a primordial matter and the essential object of our attention. It would be useless to want people to have a well-furnished mind if they lack the required health to enjoy the intellectual training which our educators strive to give them.
I am therefore in favour of extending the national hospital insurance program so as to allow all Canadians, whether poor or wealthy, the small man and the tycoon, the cultured and the uneducated man, to receive the care required by their state of health. I want Canadians from all provinces to be able to say that we, in Canada, do not waste this essential asset given us by Providence: health.
In saying this, I do not think my words are those of a specialist who cannot see beyond the limits of his field of activity, and I am convinced more than ever of the truth of the old Latin adage: mens sana in corpore sano.

Mr. Speaker, part (a), of this resolution merely suggests that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to implementing the promises made in the 1957 election and put into practice the policies which hon. members in the government party so energetically advocated when they sat on this side of the house.
My friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who as minister of national health and welfare in the Liberal administration introduced the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act in April of 1957, pointed out that the purpose of the legislation was to assist individuals only and was not designed to subsidize services provided free by the provinces. Therefore, patients receiving free treatment in provincial institutions would not be included under this act but tuberculosis patients and mental patients who were receiving care in general hospitals would be included under the benefits of the measure. Those who were paying their way in provincial institutions were also covered by this legislation.
The Conservative party at that time severely attacked the Liberal administration for not including tuberculosis and mental patients under this legislation. I could not help but notice the great contrast between the stand taken by Conservative members at the time of the introduction of the act and the stand taken today by the hon. members for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) and for Durham (Mr. Vivian). The stand formerly taken by members of that party was that by not including tuberculosis hospitals and sanitaria and mental institutions the act discriminated between physical illness and mental illness and that it was driving a wedge between tuberculosis hospitals and sanitaria and mental institutions on the one hand and general hospitals on the other.
The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was most bitter in his attack on the Liberal government of that day. His remarks as recorded in Hansard on that occasion are most interesting and I was wondering today whether the hon. members for Portage-Neepawa and Durham had familiarized themselves with the statements of their colleagues on that occasion before taking part in today's debate.
In the discussion that ensued at the time of the introduction of the act the present Minister of Finance, who was then the private hon. member for Eglinton, set forth his party's

stand in very clear terms. I am reading now from page 3380 of Hansard of April 10, 1957, where the present Minister of Finance is reported as having said:
We as a party and as Her Majesty's loyal opposition have already expressed in the strongest terms our view that there is no justification whatever for the exclusion of these hospitals and institutions from among those that lie within the scope of the scheme of hospital insurance.
The hon. gentleman's remarks previous to that clearly indicate that the institutions he had in mind were tuberculosis hospitals and sanitaria and mental institutions. During that debate the present Minister of Finance went so far as to move an amendment to the effect that the bill be referred back to the committee with the object of inducing the committee to persuade the government to amend the measure and include these institutions. In this stand he was supported by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). I will not repeat the remarks of that hon. gentleman which were placed on Hansard today by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) and which may be found at page 3386 of Hansard of April 10, 1957.
Then followed the election. During the election definite commitments were made to the people of Canada. These have already been put on the record today but I think it is well to again bring them to the attention of the house. At Winnipeg, according to a report in the Winnipeg Tribune of May 14, 1957, the present Prime Minister said:
The Conservatives, he said, would repair a "serious omission" in the federal health plan which does not include tubercular and mental institutions.
Later on in the campaign the hon. gentleman was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 28 as having said at Saskatoon:
Mr. Diefenbaker said the Conservative party still believes that hospital insurance should cover patients in mental and tuberculosis institutions.
I submit that these are very clear statements. They stand out today in very sharp contrast to the position which has been taken by the members of the Conservative party in this debate.
Following the election there was a dominion-provincial conference. During that conference there was a marked change in the stand which the Prime Minister took. He is reported as having said at that conference that he and his party had no objection to including those two institutions under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, but if that were done then the cost of these services would be deducted from any further increase in fiscal grants to the various

provinces. There clearly were no strings attached to the promises and commitments made during the election.
Nearly three years have now passed and although some hon. members opposite will still get up and say that every election promise has been kept this promise is clearly still outstanding. There was some excuse for not including these services in 1957 because then it was clearly a first step and time was needed to see what flaws would develop and what problems would emerge in the administration of the act, but whatever excuse may have existed in 1957 there is certainly much less excuse today because the plan is no longer in its first stages and has been clearly established.
The problem of mental illness is not decreasing but is getting greater and more costly every day. The distinction between physical and mental illness has also grown less. There is still outstanding what is perhaps the most tragic problem of all in connection with mental illness, the woeful lack of facilities for the treatment of children who have the misfortune to be afflicted with this illness.
Therefore the government is morally bound to implement this part of its election platform or else, on the other hand, it should admit to the people that they were wrong in advocating it and in attacking the Liberals in 1957, and they should apologize to the people of Canada for having done so.
Part (b) of this program has been in effect in my province for some time in a limited degree. I can inform my hon. friend from Portage-Neepawa that our experience has been such that the fears which he expressed today are not very well founded. It is proving a great blessing to the people, and especially to the children, because in my province it is restricted to children under 16 years of age. But it certainly has not moved us one step further forward toward the establishment of socialized medicine, which everyone seems to fear so much.
Our national health, the health of our people, certainly is our most precious asset and no one should be prevented from availing himself of medical, dental and surgical services because of financial handicaps. Therefore, I endorse this resolution.

In the fact, it could be said that the hon. member who proposed the resolution is dealing in trading stamps with the electorate. The only thing is that he is giving them red stamps instead of green. To the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), who spent a great deal of time on the remarks of the late Dr. Blair and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when they were in opposition, I would simply say this: It is too bad those remarks did not impress you when you sat on this side of the house as they do now when you are on the Speaker's left. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat said there could be no excuse for the delay in carrying out that election promise. I wonder how he explains the fact that the Liberals first promised hospital insurance in 1928, and it did not come into effect in most parts of Canada until 1958. Perhaps it was not all delay; probably changing conditions contributed to it. But my advice to them is to be patient, as you were from 1928 until 1958.
Several members have spent a good deal of time on the first part of the resolution dealing with tuberculosis and mental cases. I do not think I need to spend a great deal of time on this portion of the resolution, except to point out that the pattern of treatment is changing and today a great number of our mental patients are treated in psychiatric wards in active treatment hospitals, and many of them who are admitted to hospital receive shock treatment and are discharged before the 30-day period has expired.
As a practising dentist I am naturally most interested in the second portion of the resolution. In that regard I should like to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) who made reference to one dentist. In my opinion this was a rather cowardly act. He attempted to take advantage of his parliamentary immunity. I can only say to the hon. member that I believe the dentist made a mistake. He must have thought he was making dentures for the hon. member for Timmins and he certainly would be entitled to a much larger fee than he ordinarily receives.
The idea of insurance involves the principles of a group of people paying a premium for protection against loss, or to meet the costs of some specific item. Perhaps the

Health Insurance
resolution should be considered in that sense. Canada has made considerable progress on the road to socialized services, and instead of proceeding at a rapid pace without consideration of what we are doing I think we should stop, consolidate our position, review our program, decide what we want, what our objective is, and the best way to proceed toward that objective.
Perhaps the idea is prevalent that the Canadian Dental Association is opposed to any scheme involving health insurance. This, Mr. Speaker, is not so. I refer to a policy statement on health insurance approved at the annual meeting of the Canadian Dental Association held in June, 1956. I refer specifically to items 3 and 4 of that statement. Item No. 3 states:
The principle of contributory health insurance is approved, provided that such plan or plans assure the development of both preventive and treatment services of the highest standard and that fairness to both the recipients of the services and to those rendering the services be assured.
Item No. 4 states:
The patient must have freedom of choice of dentist and the dentist must be free to choose patients. The personal relationship between patient and practitioner is essential to a successful health service.
Item No. 3 emphasizes, first that preventive and treatment services be both included, and in preventive services would be included fluoridation, dental health education and to a certain extent the treatment of pre-school age children. But I think probably even more important in item No. 3 is that treatment services of the highest standard be retained. This is often a fault with a completely socialized scheme, that there is a tendency to cut down expenses and to give the less expensive treatment regardless of the effectiveness of the treatment.
Item No. 4, I think, is equally important in that both the patient and the dentist must have freedom of choice. In many socialized countries-in fact, Great Britain started out this way-the dentist was given a list of patients and was instructed by a civil servant that he must be responsible for those individuals and the list constituted his practice. In turn, the individuals on that list were instructed to apply to so and so for treatment and were restricted to the practitioner designated unless referred to someone else by that practitioner.
I think it would be appropriate at this time to pause and consider the number of people in Canada who are already covered by various dental schemes. The number of schemes vary in their operation and in their scope, but it is surprising the number of

people in Canada who are already covered. This list would include, of course, the Indians and Eskimos as well as the recipients of war veterans allowance. Various provinces have their own schemes. My small province of Prince Edward Island has a very good scheme when one considers the limited funds available. The province has attempted to have a number of mobile dental units visit the various parts of the province in which dentists are not available. They treat children of grade one and grade two. At the present time, there is only one operator but he has done an excellent job since joining the department. The parents of the child are requested to pay $1.50, but if they are unable to pay the child is still entitled to treatment. When the treatment is completed the child is given a certificate entitling him or her to a free fluoride treatment. The treatment is a topical fluoride treatment and is given by a registered dental hygienist.
I understand that the province of Ontario has a similar scheme for school children and, in addition, the recipients of social services are also entitled to free treatment. The various provinces, such as British Columbia and Saskatchewan, use part of their federal health grants for dental treatment. British Columbia, I understand, has two schemes, one using salaried dentists in mobile units, and the second scheme involves the use of the office and time of a private practitioner. I am told that a survey carried out by the province of British Columbia to compare the benefits and costs of the two plans indicated that the use of the private practitioner and his office was by far the most economical. Saskatchewan, in turn, uses dentists as civil servants who operate in mobile units. They, of course, spend most of their time in areas not serviced by practising dentists.
The Canadian Dental Association also emphasizes that any plan should begin with the young, and I believe that is a very wise idea because a comprehensive plan would include many people who, in the language of the dental practitioner, are classified as dental cripples. Item No. 20 on this pamphlet to which I previously referred, reads:
Variation exists from area to area as to number of children and number of practitioners which necessitates planning on an area basis. It would be unwise to institute services which could not be provided. From the preventive standpoint, complete services for a younger age group is preferable to partial services for a larger group.
Item No. 21 reads:
The growth of the plan should be determined on an annual appraisal basis, dependent on the dental health of those already in the plan, any increase in the number of practitioners and any increase or decrease in the number of children involved.

The number of various private plans in effect makes one question whether it is wise from an economic viewpoint for the government to proceed beyond a certain stage. In the United States there are a number of excellent prepaid dental plans operating very much on the system of the Blue Cross and Blue Shield in Canada. They are providing complete dental treatment at a very reasonable cost. Some plans, not of course providing complete dental care, are as low as $19 per annum, and I believe it would be extremely difficult for the government to compete with this premium. The labour unions in the United States have used a great deal of their welfare funds for medical and dental treatment. This is very interesting when one considers the attitude of labour unions in Canada, or at least certain ones, that would prefer to hand over their treasury to an unborn political party.
In the United States the unions have negotiated with various medical and dental groups to provide complete coverage for their union members and their families from welfare funds. This plan has been particularly successful in the southern United States and has completely obliterated the clamour for socialized medical and dental services in that area. The Blue Shield is still available in Canada for the medical practitioners. I think that this is an excellent plan and very reasonable in cost. I noticed that the hon. member, in moving his resolution, stated that one of the drawbacks to the present hospitalization scheme was a mix-up in hospital premiums. I do not think anyone has ever had that experience with Blue Cross or Blue Shield. It illustrates the fact that these private organizations function extremely efficiently, perhaps more so than do government plans.
This afternoon various hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield), referred to the difficulty of the medical practitioner operating within a socialized scheme. The same thing applies to dentists. In a government organization there is a tendency for the amount of paper work to keep on increasing. Forms must be filled out in duplicate and triplicate, be forwarded to various individuals for their approval and finally they end up before the treasury board of a department to be stamped. This procedure not only adds to the cost of a scheme but-what is more important-it takes the practitioner's time away from the patients. In England various practitioners were forced to discontinue their practice an hour or an hour and a half earlier than they normally did in order to complete the reams of paper work for the day.

Recently I visited my constituency and was speaking to a fellow dentist. He was complaining of difficulty in a war veterans allowance case and I think this experience illustrates the danger in these socialized schemes. A recipient of war veterans allowance presented himself at this dentist's office for treatment. The dentist filled out the necessary forms containing his recommendations for treatment and forwarded them to Ottawa for approval. In the treatment form he had recommended the insertion of partial dentures. Someone in Ottawa looked it over and wrote back saying, "We agree with you that this is a fine case for a partial denture but we do not think the man will ever wear it; therefore we cannot approve it". I think that is the big fear in the minds of doctors, dentists and optometrists, namely that we will have at the top someone who disagrees with the treatment recommended to the patient, and this results in a loss of confidence by the patient.
It might be well for us to consider the experience in other countries which have undertaken this socialized scheme of treatment. Perhaps it would be well to take a look at the experience of the British people. At first there was a great rush. Everybody wanted admission to hospital, dentures or new eye glasses. The cost of the program was extremely shocking to the British taxpayers and today we find gradual progress being made toward a stage where the patient is expected and required to pay for a certain portion of his treatment. In fact, the program got so badly out of hand in England that, as many hon. members will recall, Sir Winston Churchill, in some remarks he made during an election campaign, said that everyone had gold teeth and nothing to eat. That remark may be a bit extreme but I think it points out the danger to the treasury from these plans.
I was interested last fall to read in the Saturday Evening Post an article on Sweden. The article was entitled: "Sweden; A paradise with Problems". As hon. members know, Sweden is a highly socialized country enjoying all the so-called benefits of socialism. However, it has become very disturbing to the Swedish government that juvenile delinquency is on the increase, that alcoholism is rapidly increasing and that there has been a disturbing increase in the suicide rate. When I read that article, I recalled my history lectures at Prince of Wales College. Dr. Lily Seaman, the lecturer in history, often compared the decline of the Roman empire with socialism. As the Roman empire conquered various countries and then disbanded its army, the disbanded troops tended

Health Insurance
to collect in Rome and there was very little employment for them. The politicians of the day engaged in a game of offering free games at the forum and free grain. The more games and the more grain that were offered, the more popular was the individual candidate. The people paid no attention to the efficiency of the government. Consequently there was the decline of the Roman empire. When we are dealing with a measure calling for complete socialism, I think we should bear this fact in mind.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say this? I think we should bear in mind the consideration that any plan should be contributory and that the practitioners should be represented on the governing body. We must also bear in mind the fact that both the individual and society as a whole have a responsibility. When both the individual and society assume that responsibility, Canada will be a stronger and better nation.

I think we all agree, Mr. Speaker, that this has been a useful discussion and that we have had some valuable contributions with regard to a subject that engages the attention of many hundreds of thousands of people in this country. I am sure that the speeches of the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian), the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) who put on the record valuable information, and others, will help considerably in trying to formulate the kind of judgments and decisions we shall be obliged to take in this particular matter.
In our discussion today we have not always followed the terms of the resolution. I offer no criticism in that particular, except to say that I think it would be well at this time if we recall the resolution that has been proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
The resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing a comprehensive system of national health insurance, more particularly to give consideration to the advisability of:	(a) amending
the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act

to provide benefits on behalf of patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and patients confined to mental institutions; (b) introducing legislation to provide medical, dental and optical insurance.
The government is not being asked now by the proposer, or those who support this resolution, to make a decision on any of these points. The government is merely called upon to give consideration to the advisability of introducing a comprehensive system of national health insurance with special emphasis on the inclusion of tuberculosis sanitaria and mental institutions in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, and to provide for a system of medical, dental and optical care insurance. It would seem that it would be very difficult for the administration to refuse to accept this resolution, as all that is being asked is that the government give consideration to the recommendations embodied in the resolution.
Surely at the present time the government is giving consideration to these matters. Surely it is the responsibility of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mon-teith) and of the department which he administers to give consideration to all of these various matters. It would certainly be difficult for the minister to satisfy the house tonight that the government should not give consideration to amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to provide benefits on behalf of patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and patients confined to mental institutions.
The government could not possibly take the position that it was not prepared to give consideration to that matter, because as the hon. members for Lapointe, for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) and for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) pointed out, when hon. gentlemen now sitting on the treasury benches were in opposition they, on the occasion of the introduction of the hospital insurance act, moved an amendment to that act so that mental institutions and tuberculosis sanitaria would be included in the federal government's offer to the provinces to share in the cost of a nationwide scheme of hospital insurance. So that the minister tonight, when he replies, will not I am sure seek to defend himself by arguing that this resolution cannot be accepted on that particular count.
Hon. gentlemen opposite not only urged such a proposition but moved an amendment. It was moved by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). The Minister of National Health and Welfare cannot take the position tonight that he has not been able to persuade in particular the Minister of Finance, who has the responsibility of getting the necessary moneys to implement

this proposition, because this very amendment was moved not by the late member for Lanark but by the Minister of Finance himself. So that the government of the day, whatever its disposition about considering this resolution, cannot in all logic, and I would say in all honour, refuse to accept at least that part of the resolution.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been in office for two and a half years, and notwithstanding that they have taken no step whatsoever to amend the hospital insurance act so as to include as insurable items individuals who are patients in mental institutions or tuberculosis sanitaria. Not only did they urge this on the house when they sat in the opposition, but during the course of the election, in 1957 in particular, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), speaking deprecatingly of the hospital insurance act in many parts of the country, pointed to its weaknesses and said that if his party were returned to power he would see to it that the act would be amended so as to bring in patients in tuberculosis sanitaria and mental institutions; and we were reminded today by the hon. member for Lapointe of the very words which he used in that context.
Now it is true, as we know, that in November 1958, when the federal government as presently constituted met with the provinces, there was a suggestion that these two groups of patients could be covered by the act but that any expenditures in that regard by the federal government must be considered as diminishing any amounts of money which the federal government might extend to the provinces under the federal tax sharing arrangements with the provinces. But that was not the position taken by hon. gentlemen sitting on this side of the house when they were in opposition, and I would suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that he is in a very difficult position tonight in facing a resolution that does not call upon him to do this but merely to consider something which hon. gentlemen opposite urged when sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, when the hospital insurance act was first proposed.
Then with regard to the second part of the resolution, surely it is not difficult for the administration to accept this resolution, because, as we know, the provinces and the various bodies that meet with the Minister of National Health and Welfare from time to time-the dominion council of health and the various medical and other health associations-discuss these and other like problems and it would be difficult to believe that the minister could tonight take the position that he has not been giving consideration to these various proposals for medical care insurance.
Health Insurance
I think our objective in this country at this time, and I would take it that it must be the objective of all of us in this house, is that our primary concern is to see to it that no individual in Canada is denied the best possible medical, dental and optical care regardless of financial circumstances. That is the objective. It would be difficult surely for anyone to take the position that in this day of social progress the advantages of medical science should not be made available to everyone in this country who needs it. It would be difficult to say, for instance, that a cancer sufferer, because he or she should happen to be poor, should be denied the opportunity of getting the best possible treatment for cancer; and one could apply that principle to other diseases and to other forms of disability which may or may not attend individuals in our country.
The question is, how can we best do this? I would suggest that what often looks like a radical proposition one day, very soon as the result of the effluxion of time comes to be accepted as routine. I think of the criticisms levelled against the hospital insurance proposal when it was first enunciated, not in 1956 but, in so far as I am concerned, in 1948.
Mr. Pallet!: Do not forget what we have done.

I said "so far as I
am concerned". If the hon. gentleman wishes to be political, that is his right. I am trying to discuss a serious subject in a serious way, as the hon. member for Durham did, but maybe the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) would not understand the possibilities of that kind of approach.
In 1948, when the hospital insurance measure was proposed, there was criticism from many quarters and from many places in this country. That was socialism, they said; that was a dangerous step; that was something which would cost too much money; that was something which would destroy private enterprise; that was giving unnecessary power to the state. Today, there is not a member in this house, and there are very few individuals in this country, who would deny the validity of the hospital insurance program which now prevails in nine of our ten provinces.
This is not socialism, as I told the hon. member for Timiskaming today in an endeavour to correct him. This was simply the recognition of a principle which has been in vogue in many countries for a long time, a principle which was recognized in 1910 when Mr. Lloyd George introduced the first health insurance scheme in the United Kingdom. The criticism which arises out of abuses in

Health Insurance
the existing system in Britain represents innovations to the basic measure which was introduced, as I say, before the great war.
Thus when we consider the second portion of this resolution, let us remember this experience of the hospital insurance act; that what today may look like a dangerous innovation may tomorrow be recognized as the kind of solution which should have been provided a long time ago. The criticisms which were levelled 75 years ago with respect to secondary school education apply to these various measures which are put forward from time to time as solutions to problems which affect the people in terms of social and economic desirability.
Thus, with regard to this matter, it ought to be possible to discuss the subject without being accused of being in favour of state medicine, without being accused of socialism. Socialism means something else altogether, and it is not incorporated within the provisions of this resolution. For my part, if we can reach the same objective by voluntary effort, by private professional effort, I would see no reason for asking the community or the state to assume responsibility. The important thing is to make sure that this is done; that is to make sure that no individual is in want; to make sure that every individual in Canada, regardless of financial means, is given the best possible treatment that medical science can give. That is the principle which should actuate us. I cannot see why the Minister of National Health and Welfare should have any difficulty in accepting this resolution in the form in which it has been presented to us today. As far as this party is concerned, we have gone on record at our national convention in 1958 as follows:
The policies which the Liberal party recommends for early consideration are:
1. As a further step, to implement health insurance provision against major medical, dental and surgical expenses, which combined with hospital insurance would ensure that no Canadian would be financially crippled by illness-
We all recognize, I think, that it is possible for us in this country-for a people dedicated to the preservation of freedom-to see that freedom is maintained. No one wants to see the traditional relationship between the patient and the doctor destroyed. Most of us in this country recognize, I think, the desirability of that, and we recognize, too, the important position which the federal government has in a matter of this sort vis-a-vis the provincial governments.
We are a federal state. The ten provincial departments of health in this country are responsible for the administration of health in Canada and any effort on the part of the

central government to interfere in what is traditionally and, perhaps, constitutionally the responsibility of the provinces would properly be resented. I agree with the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Richard) that it ought to be possible to pursue this great objective which we have in mind in a spirit of co-operation, in a spirit that is consistent with the basic concepts of our confederation. No effort ought to be undertaken by the federal government which could in any way be regarded as a usurpation of provincial autonomy, provincial responsibility or provincial jurisdiction. No one has suggested that today; I mention it simply because the hon. member for Kamouraska brought this question before us, quite properly, as he would wish to do, coming from the province of Quebec.
No one suggests now, I am sure, that the hospital insurance act was an invasion of provincial rights. Yet we have heard hon. gentlemen at various times, in some quarters of this house at any rate, suggest that this was a centralizing policy, a policy designed to interfere with provincial authority and jurisdiction. Happily, now, we all recognize that those arguments had no real validity. No one wishes in any way, let me repeat, to propose anything which interferes with the basic philosophy of people in any part of Canada. All this federal government and this parliament can do is to make offers to the provinces; it is up to the provinces to accept them in the light of their considered needs and their judgment as to their capacity and desire to meet those needs.
I believe the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa was justified today in putting on the record as he did such a splendid recital of the health activities which are carried on in this country on federal account, on provincial account and through the voluntary organizations. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Durham that in a discussion of this sort we should recognize the contribution made by all the health professions, and he mentioned particularly the medical profession. It is fashionable to criticize the doctors and to say that the doctor stands in the way of progress. I had 11 years of close contact with all the health professions in this country, and while at all times I did not agree with them- and I do not agree always with them now-[DOT] in every particular, I join with the hon. member in saying that the Canadian medical profession possesses and practises standards of responsibility and social understanding as high as those of any group of doctors in any other country of the world. They will, therefore, I am sure recognize that when we consider these matters we do so not because we want to interfere with the basic integrity of a great profession but, because of the general

interest, we want to make sure that we devise those steps by which we can ensure the kind of medical care, the kind of dental care, the kind of optical care and, I may add, other forms of health care which as a result of scientific discovery, as a result of endowment, have increasingly been made possible to the people of our country and to the people of the world generally.
It must not be forgotten that the first step in health insurance in Canada was not, in so far as this party is concerned, the result of the introduction in 1956 of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. When in 1948 the national health grants were announced by the then prime minister of the day he said, as reported at page 3931 of Hansard of May 14, 1948:
I should like to make a statement to the house on government policy with respect to health services and health insurance.
Then he went on to point out that the program being announced was a necessary prerequisite to the ultimate establishment in Canada of a system of health insurance. It will be recalled that at that time the federal government decided to embark upon a system of grants in aid to the provinces. First of all there was the general survey grant which made possible an assessment by each province of its health needs. The federal government assumed full financial responsibility for the surveys that were carried on by the provinces on terms which they themselves laid down. Then followed the grants for federal public health, for tuberculosis, for mental health, for venereal disease, for the prevention and control of crippling conditions in children, for blindness prevention and control, for professional training and for public health research and, as the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa reminded us this afternoon, three other grants including the grants for rehabilitation, for child and maternal care and for laboratory and radiological services were added.
I agree with the hon. member for Durham that the general public health grant represents one of the really great achievements of that program because, as the hon. gentleman said, one of the elementary phases in the organization of attack against disease and in the building up of healthy bodies in this country is the public health unit. The public health unit has been expanded all over this country to the extent of many millions of dollars by the grant provided for by the federal government in the field of public health. What one could say about that grant one could likewise say about the improvement in mental illness, the extension of professional personnel as a result of the professional training grant, and so on.
Health Insurance
The next significant thing is that following the introduction of the health grant in 1948, which was announced as a prerequisite to a system of national health insurance, was the resolution placed before parliament on March 25, 1957 when, as a member of the government of that day, it was my responsibility to move the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize contributions to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to provinces in respect of costs incurred by them in providing insured hospital and diagnostic services pursuant to provincial law and to agreements made in accordance with the said measure, to commence when at least six provinces, containing at least half the population of Canada, have entered into such agreements and qualified for the receipt of such contributions.
I am not going to enter into any argument as to who is responsible for hospital insurance in Canada but the fact is there we have the legislation placed on the statute books of our country by a Liberal administration. No one for a moment has ever suggested that measures of this sort can be carried out only by the federal government. They represent a co-operative enterprise. The fact is, however, that with the exception of what was done in the province of Saskatchewan the only other step taken in the field of hospital insurance was taken in this house on March 25, 1957, and I believe that hon. gentlemen opposite in their effort to take political advantage one way or another would want to recognize that fact and would want to recognize the announcement of May 14, 1948 and also recognize that these measures were always proceeded with on the basis of consultation with all of the provinces in our country.
All but one of the provinces now have accepted the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, an act that now in spite of all the criticisms levelled at it is recognized as something that we should have had a long time ago, a measure-

Yes, except the province of Quebec. That is a decision for the government of Quebec. As one who lives in the province of Ontario I do not seek to tell the province of Quebec what it should do but I do hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare, consistent with his responsibilities as a federal administrator, not seeking to impose his will, nevertheless is showing some initiative in making sure that all the advantages of this federal act are being made known to those now in authority in the province of Quebec so that the government of that province can make up its

Health Insurance
mind with the greatest possible opportunity of realizing what the facts and advantages are.
The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act as it now stands made available to all persons a simple method of budgeting in advance the unpredictable costs of essential hospital care. Under this plan no one is denied benefit because of age, health or economic circumstances. No time limit has been placed on the number of days' care and so the individual is protected against catastrophic costs of protracted illness requiring hospitalization over a long period. No dollar value has been placed on the special services in hospital that may be required and because one half of the national costs of hospitalization are being paid out of the federal treasury it is possible for the provinces as we now know to offer premiums that are more attractive than those that can be charged under any existing plan.
The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act now extant in nine provinces in co-operation with the federal government provides that an individual will be free to purchase any additional protection required in terms of private or semi-private care or other special benefits through regular commercial or voluntary insurance plans.
In resuming my seat, I say there is a record behind us. We have taken an important step, one that has been recognized as being in the public interest. The resolution before us does not call upon the government to take any decision. All this resolution does is to call upon the government to consider the advisability, first, of doing something that hon. members of the government recommended when they sat on this side of the house and, second, to consider the implementation of legislation providing for medical, dental and optical insurance.
We will wait with interest the reply of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. This will be his first opportunity in a long time to make a comprehensive statement on health care. We will listen to him with sympathetic interest and, I am sure, with great anticipation.

Mr. Speaker, it is not often that I get the opportunity of following the very eminent, distinguished and eloquent member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I cannot say that my regard for him extends to accepting all the proposals that he made, and certainly I do not intend to join with him in swinging on that political trapeze which has carried him in flights of fancy into the past.
Before beginning my remarks, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Richard) on the occasion

of his very eloquent maiden speech tonight. May I say that I am very proud to be participating in this debate in that it has given an opportunity to those in the medical profession and to those of us in the dental profession to express some views other than political regarding our professions.
I am going to confine myself in the short time that was left to me by the hon. member for Essex East to some remarks regarding mental care and dental care. As we all know, mental hospitals and sanitaria are now under provincial jurisdiction and I think the closer they are to the people, the better the service is for the people. I do not believe the federal government should impinge any further upon this area of provincial activity.
Just for a moment I want to mention something that has been a very sore point with me for a long time. Before I entered the profession of dentistry I worked in the rehabilitating of mental patients, and one thing that caused me great concern-and still does because it still exists-was the matter of the committal of mental patients. After a mental patient is committed on the certificate of a physician he is brought in to the hospital by-in Manitoba, at least-two Royal Canadian Mounted Police constables. The first impact upon this patient on entering a mental hospital is most unfortunate indeed because often he is put in a strait-jacket and held up between two Royal Canadian Mounted Police constables and put into this institution which is supposed to be the hospital which will rehabilitate him. Often he is put into a small cell and subsequently he undergoes treatment by insulin shock, electric shock or both. All of these treatments seem to have a very profound effect on the patient. Indeed, it has been amazing to me that 70 per cent of them actually go back into society.
However, that was 10 years ago and I must say I am amazed at the progress that has been made in mental hospitals in the last 10 years. In fact, today in most hospitals you do not see any strait-jackets and there is very little restraint and indeed a very great deal of freedom. This has been brought about by the discovery of tranquilizers and other sedatives.
I think I had better proceed now onto giving a few suggestions regarding dental health insurance. May I say to the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), with regard to the unfortunate experience that he related today, that there are Fords and Cadillacs, and perhaps the hon. member, seeking to purchase a Ford, by mistake strayed into a Cadillac dealer.
Owing to the fact that there is very little time at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I wonder

whether I could have the unanimous consent of the house to have printed in Hansard at this point the official statement of the Canadian Dental Association on health insurance as adopted by them in June of 1956?
