speechtext:
I will pass it over, since the hon. member for Prince has already elucidated the more important points in the statement. However, in the few minutes at my disposal I want to deal with the principle of insurance as it applies to dentists. The insurance principle is based mainly on the presumption that a great number of people will pay premiums and a much smaller number will get the benefits and as such have the security which is theirs in knowing that in the event that they need the treatment it will be available on payment of those premiums. That is how the insurance principle works.
However, it cannot work when it is extended to dentistry because of the fact that dentistry is the only area of activity mentioned in this resolution which is almost universal. In fact when we find a person
Health Insurance
who has a perfect set of teeth it is cause for rejoicing and we send him down to the dental college and we investigate the type of diet he has had and we even go into his heredity and so forth, because individuals of that nature are so rare. Therefore, I cannot see how the insurance principle can be applied to dentists because if it were, then the costs of the premiums would be raised so high that people would not be willing to pay them. Therefore, we have to look for some other alternative. This is not to say that we are not in favour of health insurance, or not in favour of dental health insurance, because we have gone on record as being in favour of it provided that the right climate is there for the institution of it.
There are three things we must remember when we consider dental health, namely education, prevention and treatment. The hon. member who moved this motion mentioned it was a fact that some people in the low income groups seem to need more dental care. The one thing that we can do as a society through a system of education is educate those people to care for their teeth in such a way that treatment would be lessened. In fact, if people did a little more to take care of their teeth the incidence of dental caries could be cut in half. But it seems that the very low income people who should take a much greater interest in their oral hygiene are exactly the ones who tend to neglect it. This is most unfortunate.
Then there is the preventive program. Before we embark on a scheme of health insurance, it seems to me that there are many schemes that would benefit society greatly which have not, as yet, been instituted. One of these schemes which I should like to mention is the fluoridation scheme. Here is a scheme which at a cost of from four to 17 cents per capita per year would cut down the incidence of dental caries by at least two-thirds. As a matter of fact, the cost of fluoridation varies from area to area. In the Sudbury area it would cost about four cents per person per year, whereas in Brantford, where we have had fluoridation for a long time, the cost sometimes ran as high as 17 cents per capita. The reason for this is the type of water they have and the type of compounds that they use. However, even at 17 cents per capita this is certainly a small price to pay for dental health for the children of Canada.
For a moment or two I should like to mention a scheme that is in vogue in England. When this scheme was introduced it was found that people believed everything was free so everybody was getting dentures whenever they felt like it. They would drop them and break them, then come back for new

Health Insurance
dentures. It was soon found that in order for this scheme to work at all there had to be a nominal sum paid by each person. As soon as this scheme was instituted it was remarkable how many fewer dentures were necessary in order to satisfy the public. The thing about socialized dentistry that hurts most is the number of dental cripples that are created. I have a practice that consists mostly of children, and I have been amazed at the number of children who have come from England for whom the dental profession have yanked out teeth rather than provided adequate preventive measures. This, in essence, has created dental cripples because many of these teeth, if they had been filled at the proper time, would have saved the child a much greater expense in later life. Perhaps that is the result of conditions under socialized dentistry, but perhaps there are other reasons to be considered. However, it seems to me the dental profession in socialized countries tends to lack the same pride which we, as dental practitioners in Canada, have.
I am sure that every dentist in this country has thousands of dollars on his books representing treatments which he has rendered and for which he will never secure a dollar, a large part of it he does not expect to collect because we feel that this is a part we are playing for society. I think the great amount of work that is being done by dentists in various dental health and treatment programs which are in vogue today should not be overlooked. There are many of these treatment programs set up by service clubs. Many service clubs from various cities tend to sponsor dental clinics. They approach the dentists who work in these clinics for one morning per week for a very nominal sum, certainly much less than they could earn in their own offices. They do this because they know the need is there, and certainly they are only too happy to co-operate in this regard.
We must always consider the attitude of the public towards dental care. I know when I was in the Canadian officers training corps treating service personnel we often found soldiers and airmen for whom we would prescribe a treatment plan but they would say, no, we want our teeth pulled; we do not want them filled. This again points up the great impact education could have upon people. It seems to me if we can only educate the people to follow the proper diet they would only have to spend half the money to provide a better diet than they have today. They would have much healthier teeth.
Regardless of how a dental health insurance plan would be brought in, one of the most

important considerations would be that it be directed toward the children. The children are most important in this treatment scheme because we get incidence of dental caries at the age of two. By the age of four, 50 per cent of the children already have dental caries. So often before a child is able to care for itself or to have any realization of the impact of lack of care for his teeth he is already a dental cripple. As the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Phillips) mentioned, one of the things about which you have to be very careful is that the patient-doctor relationship is maintained. It is extremely important and when this relationship is destroyed, then I am sure the general respect for the profession would be destroyed along with it.
I could not conclude my remarks without mentioning the great advances there have been in the technology and practice of dentistry. It has been possible with the recent advances, the more modern drills and so forth, to do a great deal more work than was ever possible before. This is certainly a good sign because in many parts of the country the personnel is limited and these advances mean that many more will be able to receive treatment. Perhaps as more and more people realize that health insurance is not necessary in dentistry but that group purchase plans are the answer, groups of people such as civil service organizations or unions, will underwrite such plans. There are a great number of them in vogue in the United States and they are becoming more popular in Canada. When this day arrives we shall certainly be on our way to understanding a great deal more about this problem.
May I move the adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker?
